tree.intro: Let's walk through King's Pawn vs Sicilian Defense — White plays the King's Pawn, Black answers with the Sicilian Defense. Watch how they meet.
tree.outro: That's how King's Pawn vs Sicilian Defense plays out.

node.idea: We take White and meet the Sicilian — today we play normal theory, then deliberately sacrifice a piece and show how to fight back from a lost position.
We open the Alapin with c3.

The knight to c6 is one of the most common responses, but it's already a serious inaccuracy — not quite a mistake if Black follows up correctly, but one more slip and things get disastrously bad within five or six moves.
We strike with d4.
Black takes, capturing on d4. The knight to c6 is misplaced here for a simple reason.
The c-pawns come off on d4.
Black plays e6.
We develop the knight to c3 — though the bishop to g5 would have been a fine chance to hang it; now Black just plays...Nf6.
Black pins with the bishop to b4 — and here's our chance: we play the bishop to g5.
We play the bishop to g5 — a believable blunder, and at least it develops a piece. The comedy would be if Black declined it.
Black develops the knight to f6.
We even offer the bishop to a6 — all but begging Black to win material; it's oddly hard to give a piece away.
Black takes on c3 with check.
We recapture, bxc3.

Black wins our bishop, the pawn recapturing on a6 — the sacrifice is complete, and we've even traded off another pair of minors, making it harder on ourselves. Now the recovery begins, a full piece down. First, know this:...e5 does not win the knight back — after...h6, the bishop to h4,...g5 unpins, and if the bishop drops to g3 the knight is free. Basic, but essential.
So we play e5 — in a situation like this it's a genuine attempt to complicate the game.

Black plays h6. It slightly weakens his structure, but down a piece a small weakness isn't enough — we need something concrete. The idea is to take on f6: after...hxg5 we push to g7, and even after...Rg8 we defend the g7-pawn indirectly with the queen to h5 — if the rook grabs g7, the queen forks on h8. Recovery rarely comes in a single move: build tension and sow doubt.
We capture on f6.
Black wins our bishop, recapturing on g5.

We push to g7 and set the queen toward h5, sowing doubt. This game is really about recovery technique when you're lost, and the principles are these. Complicate — pose your opponent decision after decision, because decisions breed fatigue and doubt. Keep your pieces active — bring the rook in with h4 rather than a timid g3, and ask the "Shankland question": what happens if you just do it anyway, developing and ignoring a pawn? Defend key pawns by developing, not by a passive king move — a rook to d3 both guards c3 and prepares to lift to g3. Manoeuvre the knight toward a dream square like d6, via f7. Use a break like d5 not only to lure the bishop off b7 but to open lines and strip away defenders. And once you win material back, convert with a passed pawn — push it hard while the opponent is passive, escort it with a rook cutting off the king, and finish with the ladder-mate technique, bringing your own king up to guard the checking square so the rooks can deliver mate. Even dead lost, purposeful, problem-posing play saves a remarkable number of games.

node.idea: So we either push our own pawn to d5, grabbing the centre and chasing the knight, or just develop with the knight to c3 and the knight to f3. Black plays d5 — and the instinct is to meet it with e5, but that's inaccurate: unlike the Advance French, where Black's pawn is already on e6 giving the bad French bishop, here Black gets a good French or Caro-Kann, bringing the bishop out to f5 first and only then locking with e6.
So we take, capturing on d5, rather than allow that improved French.
The queen recaptures on d5 — transposing into a line normally reached via a different move order, and this is an isolated-queen-pawn structure.

asides.idea: Very common at the 1200-1300 level is e6. As inspiration, one of my shortest tournament games: against a 1757, thirteen moves. The engine's best is the immediate d5, but I took a slower knight to f3, still keeping an edge; the knight to f6, the knight to c3, and a decisive mistake by Black — the only way to stay alive was the bishop to b4 or d5. I was planning e5, a great Advanced French where the bishop is locked on c8 and White got the c3 developing square. Instead the bishop to b5 showed unfamiliarity, and Black was dead lost in two moves: d5, much stronger than e5, which would yield the d5 square; the trade, then d6, and the game ends — the bishop drops back to a queen-e2 check, or the pathetic bishop to e7. He tried the knight to c2 check, but I ignored the rook, brought the bishop out, pre-moved the rook to e1, and it was mate in a thousand ways.

Let's develop by the book — the knight to d2. That's the downside of the Alapin: you can't route this knight to c3. But it's fine here, and it buttresses the e4-pawn. We're clearly better, with a nice pawn centre.

We win the pawn back on d6; roughly equal. And if he pushes d5, we take, and his e5-pawn hangs — we're eyeing that pawn too.
His knight on b4 is a nice counterweight. His best was the queen to b6, preparing a rook to d8; the queen to c7 is not the most accurate.

Our knight was the vulnerable piece — so rather than use the get-out-of-jail rook to c1 to activate the rook, we've evacuated it to b5. Chess is all about priorities, and the top priority was getting that knight out.
Now our knight is safely out and defended — something we couldn't do a move ago.
He's forgotten the pawn is hanging — the knight takes on e5, and we're up a pawn. Sometimes chess is about resisting the by-the-book move and prioritising.
If he grabs on a2 he'll lose material.
We retreat the knight to c3 — an even safer square.

The rook to d8 — and we must be careful, because the queen to e1 walks into a fork. So the queen goes to a4 instead, active and pressuring his knights. When he tries the queen to c5 it doesn't actually attack our knight, because his knight on b4 would hang. That b4-knight is what cramps us, so e3 compels the trade — and with us a pawn up, trades are good, plus it removes his strongest piece. Then the finishing trick: with his queen in contact with the rook, we swing a rook to d8, and he can't defend it without a back-rank mate or giving up the rook; the queen to f5 finishes with mate to follow.

This g5 lunge shows up constantly at this level — it's meant to intimidate. But the right question is: what did it weaken? Immediately the f5 square becomes a permanent hole. So the plan writes itself — steer a knight toward g3 or e3 to occupy it.
Even without a bishop to chase, the point stands: routing the knight this way is all about earning access to that f5 square. The square is the target, not any single piece.

asides.idea: Now the strange-looking move — the knight pulls all the way back. The end goal is simple even if the route is odd: land a knight on f5. Everything is bent toward reaching that square.

node.idea: The traditional response is d5. To play it, Black has to be okay allowing e5, an Advanced French — but since I don't play the Advanced and never have, most Sicilian players are really bluffing White into e5, and often neither side knows what to do.

The more Alapin-esque way is to take on d5, and Black is at an early crossroads: recapture with the queen, transposing, or keep the e6 spirit with the pawn — and you can already see the IQP structure forming.

If Black recaptures with the pawn and White later takes on c5, Black recaptures and has an isolated pawn on d5 — the classic isolated queen's pawn. One good thing about c3: after we take on c5 and he recaptures, that c3-pawn slows the d5-pawn and controls the square in front of it, the most important thing against the IQP — controlling the square matters more than occupying it. Taking on c5 immediately is decent but not best; ideally, as in the Queen's Gambit, you wait for Black to move the dark-squared bishop first, then take on c5 to cost him a tempo.
Black plays the bishop, and then it takes on c5, so we've gained a tempo. The best and most recommended move is the bishop to b5 with check, developing with tempo —
and asking Black another difficult question.
Instead we develop and wait for a more opportune moment — the moment Black develops his bishop is a very good time to take on c5. The knight to f3.

So far, standard, well-known theory. The bishop to d6 — funnily, we can delay the pawn takes c5 one more move by castling, since Black can't resolve the central tension, but I'll stick to the traditional way.
Traditionally you take on c5 the moment Black develops his bishop —
the bishop takes c5, and we've earned a tempo, since Black made an extra move with his bishop.

Now we castle and get our king out of the centre. The next big question is where Black develops his knight — e7 or f6. Against the knight to f6, I like the bishop to g5, pinning it; but if the knight goes to e7, the bishop to g5 makes less sense.

The knight to f6 — the bishop to g5 walks into f6, and here f6 isn't so weakening we'd want to spend tempi inducing it. Important IQP ideas: the check on e1 is tempting, but Black covers with the bishop and the f2-pawn becomes a major problem — the queen to b6, or the bishop takes f2 forking king and bishop — so keep the rook on f1 to solidify f2. Two questions: where the bishop goes, which is g5, and what to do with the knight — in these structures the knight often goes to b3, hits the bishop, and heads for the blockade square.
There really aren't other options for the knight; the real decision is the order. I like starting with the bishop to g5, restricting the knight and immediately setting up a pin.
The bishop to e6. The drawback of playing the knight to d2 first —

but I don't want too many adventurous moves; I want to play traditionally to highlight our IQP technique. The knight to d2. White is slightly better — not because Black has an IQP, since you can't make categorical assertions about the isolated queen's pawn; it depends on the placement of the other pieces.
This resembles the bad-IQP case more than the good, because Black's piece activity isn't impressive — he's pinned along the diagonal, and the bishop on e6 is a passive observer tied to the pawn.
And as we play the knight to b3, we achieve complete control of the square in front of the pawn —

so the IQP is no longer a moving target; it'll saddle Black for as long as it sits on d5. Now we make marginal improving moves. Avoid the queen to d2, which runs into the knight to e4 and bad trades. The low-hanging fruit is a knight to d4 — controlling the square matters most, but occupying it isn't bad either; the knight to c4 is also on an ideal square, pressuring his minors.

The knight to d4 — I prefer the knight from b3, keeping the other knight on the kingside where it supports our king. Now we threaten to win a pawn by taking twice on c6; if the knight takes d4, we recapture with the knight.

Black's in a little trouble — hard to move, since moving the queen off d8 allows the bishop takes f6, spoiling the structure. The bishop to d7 is a good 2100 move, keeping the tension and protecting the knight. Black threatens the knight takes d4 with tactics, and the bishop takes d7 there loses a piece to the capture on f3. So we can change the nature of our advantage from an IQP to something more dynamic — my instinct is an unnatural move.

The bishop takes c6 — it transforms our advantage from a strictly positional one into an actual initiative based on superior piece activity. Two minuses: we give up the bishop pair, and, more importantly, we allow the b-pawn recapture, after which the d5-pawn is no longer isolated.

The b-pawn takes c6 — the hanging-pawn structure: pawns on c6 and d5 with no b- or e-pawn, a self-sufficient island. Think of it as the isolated pawn shifting from the d-file to the c-file: c6 is now essentially isolated, since d5 can't go backwards to defend it.

So c6 is the biggest weakness, attacked directly by the knight to e5. But the knight to e5 has other threats: taking on c6, or taking on d7 and then f6 to ruin Black's kingside structure; the bishop takes f6 also works, since the queen can't recapture. Black struggles to cover everything; the bishop takes d4 gives us a huge advantage — Black is borderline lost if he gives up the dark-squared bishop. His pieces are passive; ours are all on optimal squares.

The queen to e8 was a smart proposal, unpinning and hitting the knight. Black plays c5, which I expected, but it fails tactically to a beautiful sequence I saw when playing the bishop takes c6. Your instinct is to move the knight from d4, but the bishop takes f6 is available — the queen still can't recapture, and the knight takes d7 comes with a fork. After the bishop takes f6, the pawn recaptures, we take the bishop on d7 and claim a small edge on Black's damaged kingside — though he could tuck the king to h8 and use the g-file. There's a specific tactical line, but I need a little more time; there's a detail I missed, which may force me off my intended path.

So we resort to the straightforward path — take on f6, take on d7, and claim a small advantage based on the weak hanging pawns and the weak king. The bishop takes f6; we have to play faster given the clock.

The queen takes f6 would lose on the spot. The g-pawn recaptures. The knight to c6 here fails tactically to the bishop takes c6, the knight takes c6, and the queen to e8 — ultra-advanced tactics I'll show after the game.
The knight takes d7 — you either see these tactical details or you don't; a lot of top-level chess boils down to spotting them.
The queen recaptures. Now we have to move our knight and figure out where it belongs.

The knight to f3 I don't like, because it'd be restricted by the f6-pawn — so the knight to c2, keeping the diagonal open for the queen and able to reroute to e3 to keep harassing the d5-pawn, one of Black's main weaknesses, along with f6. White's better, not as big as I'd hoped, but only one side is having fun. The queen to f3 targets d5 and f6 and defends g2, nipping any g-file pressure in the bud, a good response to the king to h8. On Black's d4: a passed pawn is double-edged, still isolated after the trade, and we take on d4 and play the queen to f3 with tempo. The queen to f5 for Black is an impulsive blunder walking into the knight to e3 fork.

I like positions where both sides have only one minor piece — very instructive. It's not really good-knight-versus-bad-bishop, since his bishop activates with c4, but the bigger problem is all the pawn weaknesses and the flimsy king. The rook to d8 makes the king even more uncomfortable; I'd start with the queen to f3, forcing Black to contend with the threat of the queen takes f6. If Black throws in d4 anyway, after the trades I'd seriously consider not taking on f6, since it lets the d-pawn run with d3, but White's still good; the rook to d1 also works. The queen to d6 protects f6, but now the knight reaches f5 with tempo, so the knight to e3 gets even more tempting.

The queen to f3, the queen to d6. Both the rook to d1 — the measured Russian-schoolboy approach, later lifting to the kingside via d3 — and the knight to e3 are good; the knight to e3 is super juicy, since the knight to f5 with the queen to g4 and g7 could lead to checkmate very quickly. My guess is the king to h8 in response; we start with the knight to e3. The bishop to c7 is a one-move threat, met simply by g3, keeping the tension — don't give an empty check on g4, which only helps Black reach h8, and definitely don't trade queens.

node.idea: Propping the centre with c3 comes at a cost — it concedes the light squares. Once the pawns commit like this, those holes don't come back, and the opponent gets a lasting square to work with.
The d4 break is the idea here — striking in the centre when the opponent has no comfortable way to meet it. That's the lever that turns a passive setup into an initiative.
Pushing d5 and following with c4 is the structural plan, clamping down on space. It's a committal choice — these locked structures cut both ways, but the space grab is the point.

White offers the Wing Gambit with b4 — a third-string gambit with a dubious reputation. Its idea is the usual one: deflect our c-pawn off c5 so White can occupy the center with d4. But here Black is objectively better with accurate play.
We accept with the c-pawn, not the knight — taking with the knight would hand White a tempo to play c3 and prop up his center.

White plays d4 as expected, and the move on everyone's mind should be d5 — contesting the center before it's too late, and the queen can't even be hit by a knight to c3 because our pawn covers that square.

Here, though, a practical choice — the modest d6. It's probably a shade worse than d5, but it drags a theory-armed opponent onto their own thinking, and it does a fine job stopping White's e-pawn while we've lost almost no development.

We develop the knight to f6, forcing White to decide how to defend e4. Inducing the knight to c3 is a plus: it stops White from setting up c3 and d4 in the quiet, Alapin-like manner.

White plays the knight to c3. We're happy to transpose into an Open Sicilian structure once d4 arrives. Why not...e5 to stop d4? It's positionally dubious — it weakens the d5-square, and we actually welcome d4.
We play e6 — the Scheveningen structure, pawns on e6 and d6 rather than the...e5 you see in other lines.
White castles. White could instead keep the centre closed with a modest c3 or d3.
We continue developing with the bishop to e7. Against a quiet d3 we could even strike with...d5 ourselves.

White plays d4 — exactly the Scheveningen we wanted. Why not kick with...a6 first? The b5-bishop is no real nuisance and the d7-knight is our best-defended piece, so we save...a6 for a rainy day when it truly counts.
We release the tension and take on d4.
White recaptures with the queen on d4 — a queen rather than a knight in the centre, and with the rare bishop on b5, an unusual flavour of Open Sicilian.

We castle, completing kingside development. On the surface White looks better — more space, the d6-pawn a target — but the position is deceptively robust. If White ever tries the bishop to f4, then...e5 would fork it and win a piece; and Black's pieces all guard one another, so d6 is far harder to reach than it appears.
White plays the rook to d1, piling on d6 — the best move. We can delay...a6 one move more.
We play the queen to c7, completing the setup — it x-rays the c2-pawn, adds a defender to d6, and stands ready to jump to c5.

The choice sets the whole character of the game.

Setting...Qd7 aside,...Nc6 is judged the most dubious yet potentially the most rewarding;...Bd7 is the most solid but often drifts into dry, drawish positions;...Nd7 strikes the balance — sharp, offering winning chances, and still objectively sound, which is why most top players who want to win pick it.

node.idea: I'm going to play the Smith-Morra, which is kind of a scary prospect,
We take, capturing on d4. Now White has a choice — recapture, or slip into an open Sicilian with a knight to f3.
because I don't know the Smith-Morra well enough to justify playing it at this level — but if Black demonstrates superior knowledge, so be it. c-takes-d4, c3.
I'm actually happy to see the knight to f6, because this transposes the game into an
Alapin Sicilian — the move here is e5. Most Smith-Morra players are disappointed when they see the Declined Morra with the knight to f6.

The knight settles on d5, and we've reached an Alapin Sicilian by force. This is the whole point: instead of memorizing forcing Morra theory where one slip loses in five moves, we've reached a much safer, more understandable structure.

White recaptures on d4, rebuilding the center. The beauty of this whole line is that you can play it without fear — you don't have to know it to the same razor's-edge depth the accepted Morra demands.
d6 immediately, chipping away at White's advanced center. We start questioning that e5 spearhead right away rather than letting White sit comfortably.
A knight to f3 develops and props up e5. Now we have several tries — we could grab on e5 — but the cleanest is the main road.

The knight to c6 is the main, principled continuation, piling on d4 and finishing our development. Against the standard bishop to c4 there's a rare line — one Sam Shankland showed me — that really tests how deep our opponent's theory runs.
But White plays the bishop to d3 instead of c4. The pause before it tells us they're already out of book — this is just a developing move, nothing special, and crucially it doesn't do what c4 would.

So we develop the bishop to g4, eyeing the f3 knight. If White does bail out by capturing on d6, we recapture with the queen and land an ideal isolated-queen's-pawn setup, with our knight already planted on the blockading square in front of that pawn.

White does go queen to b3, we chop on f3, White recaptures with the g-pawn, and we commit to e6. Now the sharp line is queen takes b7, knight takes d4, and the check on b5 has to be reckoned with — we capture the bishop, White checks with the queen from b5, and the point I'd missed at first is that we don't have to run the king to e7; we simply block with the queen to d7, and the resulting endgame favors us because White's pawn structure is a wreck. In the game White actually declines the b7 pawn, which makes our path obvious — keep striking at the center with a capture on e5 while White still can't finish developing. The safe alternatives, a rook to b8 or the queen to d7, were both excellent; honestly the queen to d7 would have been far easier to handle. But we're playing maximally principled, trusting the complications, because our lead in development is enormous and White's whole position is on the verge of collapse.

Our knight is hanging and can't move — a retreat walks into a bishop check on b5 that's mating, and the knight on c6 will be under crushing fire. So the near-automatic move is the bishop check on b4, played essentially without further calculation, because it can only help us: it opens the door to castle kingside — a safety valve, a worst-case escape. Even in the grimmest scenario we could sacrifice the knight on c6, throw a rook to c8 with tempo, and dream of infiltrating on c1 after a knight takes c3. That's all brainstorming, not forced yet.

White blocks with the bishop to d2. The first question I ask is simply: can we castle? If yes, most of our problems dissolve and we never have to shuffle the king to f8. And there's a gorgeous resource lurking — after we castle and White grabs on c6, a rook to c8 sets up a rook lift to c1 with check that isn't a blunder, because the blocking bishop on d2 is pinned. When the king steps to e2 we scoop the rook on h1, and even if White interposes by capturing our bishop, we have one more blow: the knight swings to f4 with a nasty check and then collects the d-pawn with the queen. It all works because White's queenside has never developed.

So we castle — the answer was yes. This is why we did the hard thinking in the opening's first ten moves: now the play is straightforward, and White is simply lost if the calculation holds. Once a queen takes c6 fails to that rook lift, White's position caves in; his queen goes from greatest asset to greatest liability — stranded offside on the queenside, unable to rejoin the game or defend the loose points scattered across the board. White can't even castle safely: a capture on d2 with a queen check on g5 rakes in the minor pieces, and our knight leaping to f4 hits g2 with mate ideas.

White tries a rook to g1. Now we shift from sharp tactics to simple technique. Our knight isn't really hanging — we can leave it on c6 — but why would we, when it has a dream square on d4? After the knight lands on d4 we've checked the ideas: if White captures our bishop, we recapture, and should the queen take on b4 our knight jumps to f3 forking the king and rook while unmasking a discovered hit on the d3 bishop. White can't hold everything together.

We take on d4, and there's nothing to fear — a bishop lunge to h6 at g7 is simply illegal, and there are no pieces near our king for White to attack. The one thing to avoid is pushing the f-pawn, which would allow a lateral back-rank mate. White's best try to stave off the doom is a bishop to e4, since it guards the sore f3 pawn; there's no easy way to hold f3 otherwise. Meanwhile we can pile up on the queenside with a rook to b8 or even set about trapping that stranded queen with a quiet a5.
White does defend with the bishop to e4. Now we just maximize — and the straightforward path is a rook to b8, bringing our last piece into the attack with tempo against the offside queen.

The rook swings to b8. From here it's take the bishop, take the b2 pawn, and our rook roars into the attack while White's queen is hopelessly stranded on a7 — it did its job snatching b7 and a7, but now it can't get home. When you sense the win is close, don't hunt only for mate: look for the move that wins material outright. A knight to c3 is the cleanest, hitting the rook and preparing tactics down the file. There are a dozen winning tries — a queen to h4, a knight to f4 — but the discipline is to choose simple, healthy moves and never blow it chasing a brilliancy: a flashy queen check that lets the king slip out can hand back the whole advantage. White is completely cooked and resigns.

asides.idea: Whenever you play the bishop to g4 in the Alapin, for either color, you learn to watch for the blindsiding queen to b3. Once our bishop leaves the back rank, the b7 pawn loses its guard and the knight on d5 is undefended — so a queen to b3 lunges at both loose targets at once. But here it just isn't that scary. We have several answers. We can throw in a capture on f3 first — White should recapture with the g-pawn, because grabbing b7 with the queen runs into a knight jump to b4 hitting the queen. Yes, trading our light-squared bishop carries some risk, but White's center is so brittle that ruining the pawns around it is well worth the bishop. Then we choose a calm follow-up: either e6 — sacrificing b7 but cementing that d5 knight and preparing to fianchetto — or the safe retreat of the knight to b6, killing two birds by guarding b7 and stepping to safety. The critical line runs e6, queen takes b7, knight takes d4, and a bishop check on b5 leads by force to a better endgame for us, because White's shattered pawns tell in the long run. Calmer souls can just play a rook to b8 or the queen to d7 — pure Soviet-schoolboy moves — and stay completely fine.

node.shortIdea: The knight to c6 is the main, principled continuation, piling on d4 and finishing our development.

asides.idea: Here's why bishop to d3 matters. Our instinct is to trade on e5 and open the center, because when White misplays the Alapin he often bites off more than he can chew. And notice the difference: if the bishop were on c4 and we captured on e5, our knight on d5 would already be hanging — from d3 it isn't, so we've effectively been gifted a tempo. We don't rush the immediate bishop to g4 though, because that hands White a bailout with a capture on d6; and after a trade on e5, White can also answer with a knight taking on e5 and things get very sharp. It's important in such a position not to rest on your laurels — a lot of people win a piece and then get very disoriented. There are essentially two ways to think here: one is to play it very safe, just get your bishop out and castle, and there's nothing wrong with that; but if you want to play for maximum, consider a move like the knight to e4 — the knight to g4 is also very interesting, and then the bishop to c5, with ideas of developing a smothered mate.

Between the knight to e4 and the knight to g4, I like the knight to e4 more, because it also closes the e-file, so White can't defend the f2-square with check — he can still defend f2 with his queen, but not with check — and this arrangement creates all sorts of tactical concepts. The bishop to g4 is an interesting idea: the bishop to g4, the queen takes g4, and we're very close to the queen to g1 with check, and if the rook takes g1 there's mate on f2 — but after the bishop to g4, the queen to g4, the queen to g1, there's the king takes. So you set it up: h5 to prepare the bishop to g4, or, more elegantly, the bishop to c5, which also prepares the bishop to g4 — and I think we win precisely that way. He plays h3 — a good move — but now we can take it to the next level: since we haven't castled yet, we can use that to our advantage with h5, and now the bishop to g4 is a threat, because after h-takes-g4 you recapture with the h-pawn, which is a check against the king, essentially checkmate. And there we go, the bishop to g4 — a total beatdown; that's why you need an opening repertoire at this rating. The queen to e3 is a nice move I honestly didn't see, but let's decline the draw; our instinct here should be to simplify. The moment he played h3, you should have noted that the g3-square is now a weakness — so in your mind, if the queen ever moves away from f3, there's a fork on g3. Combining that observation with this position, the simplest is just to take the queen and then deliver a nice little fork on g3 — we'll be up a rook, and the rest is really easy.

node.idea: The early queen sortie is the amateur try — and rather than the automatic developing move, there's a way to maximise the advantage: the knight jumps to e5. It isn't quite a fork, since the bishop can escape, but it grabs the bishop pair early and drives the queen onto a horribly exposed square.

Now expand and put that uncontested light-squared bishop to work. Prefer e6 over the natural pawn move for two reasons: it readies a central break — one you won't rush, since opening the centre just for its own sake is unwise — and the bishop is destined for the fianchetto anyway, so it won't get trapped behind the pawns.

Against the central push there's a nifty device to blunt the opponent's dark-square grip — the simple central knight move is fine, but the pawn to d5 is stronger, and if a queen check comes it can be met by a block or by dropping the knight home to d7.

No reason to trade queens with such a lead in the centre and in development. And when the queen's escape route gets closed off, file it away — start hunting for ways to exploit its vulnerability for queenside gains, and, if the opponent is careless, to trap it outright.
Turn the queen's awkwardness into space — a rook-pawn nudge to a6 chases it, and then b5 does double duty: it builds an imposing pawn mass and prepares the fianchetto onto a gorgeous long diagonal.

When the opponent pushes back on the queenside, the sharpest reply is the immediate fianchetto — and it isn't even a sacrifice. Playing Benko-style, if the b-pawn is grabbed the bishop swings to a6 to press the weak d3-pawn, and without calculating a step further you can trust that there's full compensation, most likely more.
It's not even necessary to go that route — a queen check on a5 forks the king and the loose pawn. Turning the opponent's own aggression into a tactic is the cleanest path.

node.idea: Against offbeat play the recipe is to follow principles to the letter — just develop, and there's only so much harm the opponent can do. The knight comes to f6, and the central push is already denied, since that square is guarded — which is exactly why the other knight came out first.
The centre-fork trick is available — capturing in the centre and regaining the piece with a pawn break — but here it's premature and leads to needless complications. A calmer path is better.
So play e6 instead, quietly preparing to expand with the central break. The fork trick doesn't vanish — it stays in reserve, ready depending on how the opponent develops.

Against a second-rate opening, play principled chess and punish it — the pawn to d5 grabs the centre and takes the fight to the opponent, rather than drifting. Seize the initiative when the opening invites it.

Priority now is kingside development, since the king is still central and the opponent is signalling a quick castle. But there's a subtlety — they also intend a central push, and sleepwalking into the recapture would leave an isolated queen's pawn, with the opponent controlling the square in front of it and that bishop suddenly justified. Meeting the push yourself is an option, though it too has a real cost, opening that bishop's diagonal.

e5 isn't great, but the Najdorf holds a special place in Sicilian players' hearts: a6. The most immediate idea is to cover the b5-square, stopping the knight from going to b5.
The bishop to e2 — one of the most popular responses to the Najdorf, considered among White's quietest options; quiet in the proper context, not boring.
e6 leads to the Scheveningen structure, but I've always been an e5 player. If you don't play the Najdorf and this move doesn't seem weird to you, then you're doing something wrong.

Why does the knight to b3 look like a big positional mistake, when it's the theoretical move? Because e5 weakens d6 and correspondingly the d5-square. This is precisely why I don't recommend the Najdorf to beginners — you have to earn the right to violate these basic rules by knowing them first; practice violating them too early and you build a rotten foundation. There isn't one single reason Black gets away with e5 — it's a very complex network of reasons.

First, we develop and get our king out of the centre — the bishop to e6 is possible, but the main move is the bishop to e7, preparing to castle as early as possible, and the c8-bishop might later fianchetto to b7. The first of the reasons d5 isn't the end of the world: Black has a lot of pieces to contest d5 —

you can put the bishop to e6, and the knight on f6 is supported by its brother on d7, so two pieces directly and one indirectly control d5, making it incredibly hard for White to plant and hold a knight there in practice, with Black's pieces clustered on the kingside.

That's reason one why the weakness of d5 isn't as devastating as it looks. Reason two: Black has counterplay on both sides of the board, one source being the b-pawn advance to b4 — though games have been lost by letting a knight sit on d5 all game; I once mishandled it and lost. Now we deploy the bishop to e6, adding another protector to d5; the queen to d3 is a legitimate try. Against the bishop to g5, the knight to d7 is correct — it's very hard to dislodge the f6-knight, and if he takes we retake — and all four minors are clustered, ready for queenside operations. He drops the knight, a blunder, and I take it, up a piece; part of the benefit of playing what most people don't is that unfamiliar positions cause blunders. We keep making Najdorf moves: the rook to c8, a typical Sicilian move pressuring the knight, sometimes with an exchange sac on c3; h6 to tickle the bishop and make luft. The bishop drops to d2, x-raying the queen, so we move the queen — since our rook is on the c-file, the queen to c7, queen and rook on the c-file, very common in the Najdorf. What does doubling do when the knight isn't hanging? Pressure — the knight can't move because pieces fall behind it. Then b5, expanding on the queenside and making an outpost on c4 for a knight, bishop or queen, and the queen gets access to b7 to pressure e4. The ultimate goal is d5, prepared flexibly: not the knight to b6, which with b3 played has no c4 prospects, but the queen to b7 — flexible, a standalone good move pressuring e4 and threatening the knight to c5. Then the knight to c5, the knight takes c4 winning the pawn, and d5 in the best version. On the recapture on e4, we trade queens to simplify while up a piece, since he can't move the queen without dropping the bishop; the knight takes d4 pins us, but White can't exploit it because d5 supports the knight next move — the queen takes e4 is great. He gives up the bishop, two pieces down, and resigns. The knight to a5 was the decisive blunder.

asides.idea: Let me show my most painful experience with e6, from the 2006 Pan-American Championships in Ecuador against Jorge Cori, now a grandmaster over 2650 but then, like me, a bright-eyed 2000. e6 looks the same as e5 without weakening d5, so what's the drawback? A few: it obstructs the bishop, which must fianchetto or reroute via d7; the e6-pawn becomes a target of White's typical f4 and f5 plan; and Black is very cramped, making it hard to defend against kingside attacks, whereas e5 makes it literally harder for White to attack. Watch how I make normal moves — castle, the knight to c6, the queen to c7, the rook, the bishop to f8, the rook to b8 for b5, the knight to a5 toward c4, g6 to blunt the queen — and then he plays e5, which would have been impossible if my pawn were on e5, and follows with a sick move, a bolt from the blue, winning on the spot, because all of Black's pieces are cramped and the king is weak, so White simply slams a knight onto d5. The knight takes d5, the bishop takes d5, pressuring f7, and if the knight takes e5, the rook takes f7 wins the queen and mates anyway. He demolished me. That's a come-to-papa system — e6 and d6 invite White to come at you; I'd rather be the one coming to papa, with more space, which is why I don't like e6.

He's good, not going down without a fight, but you can see the cracks beginning to show. Now is a great time to show why we deployed the knight to c2: there's a move I call a glue move — a move that glues together all the disparate parts of White's position; it stops the queen from attacking b2, lends further support to the bishop, and just glues everything together nicely. That's the knight to b4. Note that b2 was hanging — f2 isn't hanging, because it's protected by the king. Now we have time for simple prophylaxis: where's his knight going? To f4, obviously — how do we prevent it? By going g3. A good observation is that the d5-square is also free, but we don't want to rush a knight there, because the knight on b4 is fulfilling the crucial role of defending b2. He goes back, and now we complete our development by castling. He plays f5 — a lot of people would worry about him opening the file, but understand the drawback of pushing the f-pawn when castled: you weaken the diagonal, so this check on c4 might be very strong in a couple of moves. Let's take on f5, and if he takes back, we make a discovered check and his knight is lost. He can't recapture on f5 — well, he did, but this knight is defended by the rook, and that rook also defends the other rook, so it's overloaded, and by giving the check we expose the tension of the rooks. Boom and boom — we're up a knight and a pawn, and we're winning. The most important moment in the game was g3 — it frustrated him, he got impatient trying to create counterplay, and he fell apart very quickly. Let's capture the knight, and now, notice, the bishop and the queen can combine in a battery threatening checkmate, and his bishop on f6 is going to be lost as well, because to defend against it he has to give it up. He runs, we take; how do we keep harassing the king after it moves to f7? Notice the knight to d5 could be a fork. The bishop to c4 or the bishop to g6 are both good. Our goal is to get the king onto e7, a forkable square, so we assess all the checks we can make, including retreating moves — people often miss retreating moves, and they're the glue that makes an attack run. The bishop to g6 cuts the king off from f7; the queen to h3 forces the king onto e7, literally the only move, and that king walks right into the fork with the knight — we win the queen and the game. We didn't do anything extraordinary: we played the theoretical moves and he collapsed quite quickly.

The Baltic is the bishop to f5 — the whole point is to develop this bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain before playing e6. The critical try is queen b3, which develops the queen and hits b7. node.idea: The knight to f6 is the Marshall Defense — a cross between a Grünfeld and a Queen's Gambit Declined that simply doesn't work, though White must be precise to prove it.
We take on d5 and Black recaptures with the knight, exactly as the Marshall intends.
The strongest reply is e4, kicking the knight and grabbing a broad pawn center at once.

Now the move you have to know: the bishop to d3. It looks quiet, but the natural knight to c3 is actually a mistake — it walks into e5, when the queen trade with check leaves White scrambling. Bishop to d3 sidesteps all of it and keeps the edge.
We develop circumspectly with h3, so a bishop to g4 can always be met by f3 — a small luxury we can afford because Black burned tempi shuffling the knight around.
Rather than the passive bishop to e3, we go to g5 — the pawn on d4 is already held by the knight, so we spend the bishop on pressure instead of defense.
The simplest plan: go after the fianchetto bishop. The queen to d2 prepares the bishop to h6 — trade that bishop and Black's king weakens and his grip on d4 loosens.
When Black lunges with c5 we don't take — that would justify his whole setup. We push d5, jamming the door shut and keeping a protected passer.
Black recaptures on e5, and note the risk in that: once a fianchettoed bishop ventures off g7, it can struggle to get home, leaving holes and inviting f4.
So the bishop to h6 makes him regret it, cutting the bishop off from its return square.
There's no rush and no reason to wait — we take on g7 and strip the king's defender.
The rook belongs on d1: if Black frees himself with e6 and the pawns come off, that rook stacks behind the queen down the d-file.

node.idea: g3 is the move that defines the Catalan: the bishop heads to the long diagonal, raking across d5 and the queenside.
The Catalan bishop settles on g2, and the whole opening is built around its pressure down that diagonal.

With a6 Black prepares to grab on c4 and hold the pawn with b5. So we protect the c4-pawn the Catalan way — the queen to c2, which guards it without blocking a single developing piece — and we'll bring a rook to d1 to keep the d4-pawn solid. From here the entire battle turns on one break: Black wants c5, trading his backward pawn and equalizing; we spend the middlegame preventing it. The bishop to g5 discourages it by overloading the piece that guards both f6 and c5, and once c5 is stopped for good we grind down the half-open c-file — that slow squeeze is what makes the Catalan so unpleasant to face.

node.idea: The Queen's Gambit Declined is the ideal beginner's opening — a gateway into a whole world of classical play. The traditional developing move is the bishop to e7, but there's a sharper try for a little extra edge, one that looks for all the world like it hangs a pawn.
That try is the knight to d7 — and the point is a trap plenty of players walk straight into. It makes a perfectly sound theoretical move while quietly laying a snare.
Round out the kingside by castling short — get the king safe before committing the rest of the army.

Here's the offbeat gem — the simplifying system. Instead of the usual queenside fianchetto, play the modest c6. Be warned, it looks bad: passive, and it does hem in the light-squared bishop. But there's a method behind the passivity.
Now the paradox pays off — capture on c4. Because the exchange was delayed until the opponent's light bishop had already committed, recapturing it costs them a tempo. Patience turns into a free move.

node.idea: exd5 gives us the Carlsbad structure — a subtly imbalanced formation, named for the city where it appeared in the great early-1900s tournaments, with a lifetime of ideas inside it.
The first Carlsbad move is c6, reinforcing the d5-pawn that anchors the whole structure.

Be7 breaks the pin — the dark bishop's usual square here, though d6 is possible — and h6 can go in any time but isn't obligatory. Then castle, and start the key Carlsbad maneuver: Nbd7 to guard the f6-knight against Bxf6, then Re8 and Nf8, from where the knight both heads to g6 or e6 and defends h7.

node.idea: With the king already flushed out, the recovery plan is to castle by hand. The king doesn't have to hurry straight back — first complete development, then walk it to safety step by step.

Two routes present themselves: simply retreat the king toward e8, or fianchetto and shepherd the king to f8 by hand. The catch with the fianchetto is a pawn to b3 followed by the bishop swinging to a3 — that diagonal shot freezes the king in place and stops the manual castle.
So play g6 with a contingency in mind — meet b3 with the fianchetto, and if the bishop lunges to a3, just drop the king back to e8. Every setup has its own answer.
The rook goes to e8, not f8 — putting it on f8 would jam the king's own escape route. With the file cleared, the king can march to f8 and onward to g8, and the by-hand castle is done.

All those tempi spent, it's time to hit back in the centre. The opponent's kingside build-up looks imposing but it's flimsy — leave it untouched and it becomes total positional domination, so it has to be challenged.

The pawn storm looks scary but isn't — the setup is rock-solid, and if the h-pawn captures on g6 it's simply recaptured with no damage. Understanding that the structure holds is what lets the counterplay proceed calmly.

Here's the counter-intuitive call: yes, capture again on c4. Most of the time the cautious answer would be to hold off, but not here — it saddles the opponent with an isolated queen's pawn on d4, and the queen immediately leans on it. Opening the centre also pulls the opponent's focus away from the kingside attack. Best of all worlds.

Now bring out the last knight. One plan is the slow route — reroute it toward the blockade square in front of the isolated pawn. The more direct plan is to send it to c6 and trade off the opponent's strong advanced knight as fast as possible.

node.idea: The Chigorin — Nc6 against the Queen's Gambit, a committal, aggressive sideline that goes straight for White's centre. Think of it as the Scandinavian of 1.d4.
The whole idea is to pile pressure on the d4-pawn immediately — dawdle and you're lost in five moves.
e5 is the only move — the decisive central strike that makes the opening work.

Against e3 — a passive try — we develop actively with Bg4, adding another attacker to d4. And the key detail to remember: if White plays Nc3, we have Bb4 to neutralize it; without that resource the whole line collapses.
Castle long and look at the pressure crashing down on d4 — this really is a good Scandinavian, where the queen goes to h5 instead of a5.
Qh5 is the thematic square: once White castles, Bd6 piles onto h2 for a quick mating attack — and the b4-bishop has done its job, since d5 is no longer a threat.
White's d5 is bold but bad — he's simply not developed enough to hold it. Nf6 wins the pawn, since dxc6 fails to the pin.

Take the pawn — no calculation needed, just see the pin and the loose rook. Then Bxf3 is the instructive move: strategically it hands over our fine bishop, but tactically it's justified, clearing the e-file to hit the uncastled king with Qe5-check hitting the king and the knight. Chess is a constant interplay between the strategic and the concrete.

node.idea: e6 quietly shores up the d5 pawn, giving the centre a firm second layer of support before anything else develops.

Both sides play this modest pawn move, and it carries a real drawback worth naming: it hems in the queen's bishop. It isn't a mistake — just a conservative way to build, trading a little piece activity for solidity.
c5 strikes back at the centre, refusing to let the position settle into something one-sided. Contesting the middle early is the whole idea.

The centre becomes a little interlocked box of pawns — it looks tangled but it's beautifully balanced, every unit propped up by another. Because nothing can be won by force, neither side wants to be the one to flinch and release the tension.
The tension finally breaks — capturing on c5 is a decision to clarify the centre rather than keep sitting on the standoff.
This little rook-pawn nudge is preparation, not an end in itself — it's clearing the way for a pawn to expand on the queenside with b4.

The point of the earlier rook-pawn move now shows: it discourages a pawn from lunging to b5 to harass the knight, because the answer would be to capture on b5 and rip open the a-file. A small prophylactic move that quietly rules out the opponent's plan.

Why isn't the pawn just hanging for free? Because loose pieces drop off. The move order is everything — capture the knight first, and then the recaptured queen is left a sitting duck: a check springs in from b4, forking and collecting it. Snatch the pawn in the wrong order and the trick evaporates.

node.idea: The modest pawn to e3 is the Colle — a very solid opening, but the reply doesn't change one bit: just play the Queen's Gambit Declined setup no matter how the opponent arranges the pieces. Let their choice be the one that has to adapt.

Notice what jumps out — the opponent hasn't developed a single kingside piece, and the standard punishment for that is to open the centre. It isn't easy here, since the direct breaks are covered, so rather than the slow preparation there's a sharper way to make the key break possible.
That way is to undermine the pawn with a5 — a typical response in countless openings, hitting the base of the queenside advance. Even if it's captured, the freeing break becomes available anyway.
The opponent's move drops the pawn — so capture, but take the hanging rook first, since it's the piece under attack. Resolve the loose material before collecting the winnings.

Facing the bishop, most instincts say you must trade — but there are ways to swap on your own terms or even decline. Keeping the tension with the queen out, ready to trade but demanding the queen reach an active square, is one option; the knight development has the downside of blocking a pawn.

The best move is the central break c5 — it carries two ideas at once. If it's captured we can't recapture immediately, since the bishop x-rays through, but the break's real gift is that it opens a path for another piece to join in.

That other piece is the queen, swinging to a5 to pin the bishop — now capturing on the queenside would lose the queen, so the opponent's retreat is absolutely forced. The break didn't win the pawn; it opened the line that wins the game.

A perfect illustration of not assuming you must trade — the bishop is simply taken, keeping the queens on the board because the enemy king is stuck in the centre and the other bishop can barely develop. Keeping the strongest pieces on multiplies the winning chances.

The king is stranded, so open the centre as fast as possible — the d-file is the avenue of attack, the pathway that leads straight to the king. Identify that main file or diagonal early, because you simply cannot attack without open lines.
When a knight parks itself on a strong central square, the first instinct should be — can it be kicked? Here the pawn push to e5 does exactly that, evicting it before the rook swings in with check.

The best development comes with check — the bishop to f5, hitting the exposed king. It's almost mate, forcing the only defence, and the whole point is that the threats against the king vastly outweigh a hanging bishop of one's own.

Recapture in the centre with the knight, unmasking a devastating discovered check — and if the opponent trades, the bishop finishes it. The material left hanging elsewhere is irrelevant next to a forced mate.

A piece of attacking wisdom — be wary of checks delivered right up against the enemy king. A rook check at close quarters lets the king sidestep and suddenly ties your own knight to the very rook you just planted. The king is a pesky defender, so attacking from a distance is often stronger than crowding your pieces next to it, where they can get loose.
And the clean finish is the queen check on b4, the king driven to the corner, and a rook to the back rank delivers mate — the simplest, most accurate path home.

node.idea: The Carlsbad is defined by this early trade on d5 — instead of the traditional Bg5 main line with the pawn left on c4, we release the tension right away.

After Black recaptures we reach the Carlsbad structure: White's e-pawn against Black's c-pawn, with everything else symmetric. That small imbalance is what generates rich positional — and often sharply tactical — middlegame play.
We handle it like a normal Queen's Gambit Declined — the bishop to g5, e3, the standard moves — and let the structure dictate the game later.

Starting with the queen to c2 stops an annoying bishop to f5. When Black develops to the inaccurate d6 rather than e7, we go for the classic plan: install the Pillsbury Knight on e5, braced by the d4-pawn and a pawn to f4 — a construction many players simply can't handle. If Black challenges it, f5 nets a full minor piece for two pawns, and with our two bishops raking an open board we castle queenside and grind, seizing the only open file.

node.idea: In the Accepted there are two fundamentally different roads — the solid one built around a modest pawn move, or the aggressive central grab with e4. The big centre isn't the only move, or even the main one, but it's considered the most testing.
The rook-pawn move is odd — it just lets the pawn be recaptured, and in this line every tempo matters. Facing passive play, there's nothing exotic to do; simply develop the pieces cleanly.

Follow your instincts — capturing would only invite a queen trade, so the obvious move is to push to d5, grabbing more of the centre and building tension. If it's exchanged, a knight lands on a beautiful central outpost.

A very instructive moment — many players see the knight tension and assume they must react, breaking the position or lunging the queen out. It's a false alarm: nothing is actually threatened. A capture is met by recapturing with the bishop, which is just as good, and grabbing the central pawn would be catastrophic, opening the file for a rook and a decisive pin. So develop as if nothing happened, because nothing did.

The opponent blunders — spot the standoff, the two queens facing off with the king tied to defending its own. Distract that defender with the classic bishop check on f7, and the queen falls. A queen guarded by only one piece is always susceptible to exactly this kind of shot.

Do run the safety check first — after the king takes, make sure there's no in-between check that saves the defender. Here that resource is blocked by the opponent's own pawn, so the queen is simply won and the game with it.

tree.intro: Let's walk through King's Pawn vs Caro-Kann Defense — White plays the King's Pawn, Black answers with the Caro-Kann Defense. Watch how they meet.
tree.outro: That's how King's Pawn vs Caro-Kann Defense plays out.

node.idea: We have Black against a strong opponent and play a very conceptual opening — the Caro-Kann, answering the king's-pawn with the pawn to c6.
White plays the pawn to d4 and we meet it with d5.
White captures on d5.
We recapture with the c-pawn — the Exchange Caro-Kann.

White develops the bishop to d3 — the Exchange, one of the most reputable lines: very solid and London-like, with the bishop on d3, the pawn to c3, and the other bishop to f4. Black's setups all revolve around finding a home for the light-squared bishop, which, as in the French, often struggles for a good square — and if White plays h3, its development gets badly restricted.
So the soundest choice is the knight to f6 first, rather than the natural knight to c6 — and if White plays c3, we develop the bishop before it can be shut in.
White plays the pawn to h3, restricting our bishop — so we revert to a different plan.
We develop the other knight to c6. And if White plays c3, we have an interesting line that gives Black a very active game.
White plays the pawn to c3. The principal reply is the pawn to e5 — punishing White for not developing the king's knight early enough.
The pawn to e5 — this is real theory, not spitballing. It most likely leads to an isolated queen's pawn structure for us on d5.
White captures on e5, and we get the IQP structure — a good chance to talk about handling the isolated queen's pawn.
We recapture with the knight on e5.
White plays the knight to f3 — the best line. Now we decide what to capture.

The plan, step by step. The bishop pair is worth keeping active, so we take the light-squared bishop — the knight takes d3 with check, and the queen recaptures. Now the dark-squared bishop: e7 is too passive and c5 runs into the check on b5 that provokes the awkward knight to d7, so the right square is d6 — safe and eyeing the kingside. In an IQP position, whoever controls the square in front of the isolated pawn is better, and that's White on d4 — but our compensation is the bishop pair in an open position with fine coordination. If White plays the bishop to g5, we answer the pawn to h6, sacrificing the IQP for an open game and the two bishops. After the trade on f6 we recapture toward the centre — never with the g-pawn, which would wreck our structure. Then the rook swings to d8, an x-ray on the queen forcing it off the centre, and since White's queenside is undeveloped we pour on the initiative: the bishop to f5, ignoring the b7-pawn, chasing the queen around — the queen has almost no squares, and there's a recurring bishop-h2 back-rank motif because we still control the luft square even after White's h3. The deepest idea is the bishop to c2 setting up the retreat bishop to d6 to trap the queen. When we finally win the extra piece, we convert cleanly: simplify with a rook trade, force the queens off with the queen to e6 while keeping the bishop attacking the knight, then the deep freeze — the pawn to b5 to freeze White's queenside pawns so the dark-squared bishop can pick them off, trade the light bishop for the knight, and mop up.

tree.intro: Let's walk through King's Pawn vs French Defense — White plays the King's Pawn, Black answers with the French Defense. Watch how they meet.

node.idea: We open with the king's pawn and Black declares the French.
We take the full center with the d-pawn — the invitation the French always accepts.
Black strikes at our center with d5. This is the defining tension of the French: the pawn on e4 has to decide its fate.
We choose the Advance — lock the chain and take the space. The pawn on e5 cramps Black's kingside and hands us a long-term spatial edge; the whole game will be about who breaks the chain first.
Instead of the near-universal c5, Black tries the rare b6, planning to reroute the light-squared bishop to a6 and trade off the French's famously bad bishop before it gets buried behind the chain.
Here's the clever touch: the quiet c3 first. It looks like nothing, but it lays a trap for the immediate a6 trade — and the reason is worth pausing on.
Black finds the correct reply, tucking the queen to d7 rather than grabbing the trade at once.
We develop the bishop to d3, its best diagonal in the Advance — aimed straight at Black's kingside where our space advantage will tell.
Black carries out the plan with the bishop to a6, offering to swap off the light-squared bishops.

The key decision — and the move most players get wrong. Not the natural Nf3 but the knight to e2, because it leaves the f-pawn unobstructed. That is the whole strategic key to the Advance: once we castle we want the thematic f4-f5 break to storm the kingside, and a knight on f3 would block it. From here the plan writes itself. Black concedes the light-squared bishops but loses tempi doing it; when he lunges with h5 he only hands us a weak square on g5 that we'd occupy with the dark-squared bishop — and we don't rush h4 ourselves, we wait for Black to push it and then freeze it with h3, since a pawn that comes to h4 becomes a target once our knight reroutes to g3 and later f3. On the queenside we play the advanced-French idea a3 and b4 to force the c-pawn to commit, prying open the c-file to double rooks, with a prophylactic h3 to deny Ng4. Then the classic finish: having won the queenside, we swing the queen to the kingside and play on both wings at once, where Black is most exposed.

node.idea: Black strikes at the base of the chain with c5 — standard fare. Most players now automatically prop the chain with c3, entering heavy theory.

But my recommendation slips through the cracks — the Nimzowitsch French: the knight to f3, developing as if nothing's wrong, letting Black wreck our pawn chain by taking on d4. It seems utterly counter-intuitive to allow that, even to sacrifice the d4 pawn, which is what we'll do.

Black develops the knight to c6. We keep developing as though Black exerts no pressure on d4. One common beginner mistake here is the bishop to b5 — not because it drops a piece, since after a queen-a5 check there's the knight to c3, but conceptually: the bishop on b5 is a paper tiger, and Black just blocks with the bishop to d7.

The best square for our bishop is d3, for several reasons. With a pawn on d4 like this, placing the bishop behind it is good practice: if Black castles kingside — the likeliest direction — we'll have a Greek-gift sacrifice ready.
Now — doesn't Black just have c4, hitting the bishop?

They do, and we retreat the bishop to e2 — but we've PROVOKED c4, and with the centre relatively closed we can afford to move the same piece twice. What did provoking c4 achieve? It took the pressure off d4 — our chain is safe now — so we can focus on completing kingside development.

Black's queenside pawns look imposing, and b5 is actually a good move — but Black has bitten off more than she can chew, pushing all those pawns without piece support. We'll use OUR pawns, a very typical idea, to break down the whole chain.
We pressure both the c4 and b5 pawns at once: b3 hits c4, and we'll follow with a4 — classic pawn play to demolish Black's chain as fast as possible.
Black plays the queen to b6.
We don't even castle first — we play a4 at once, and Black is under serious fire on the queenside. One key tactical detail: a6 is futile here.
The bishop to a6 is powerful — our opponent tries to shield the chain with the minor pieces, but they're just not good at keeping a pawn chain intact.
Which pawn first? Normally you start at the base — a takes b5, capturing on b5, removing the linchpin.
Black recaptures, capturing on b5. Now step two: take on c4, opening the centre and leaving a major weakness there.

We complete the trade, capturing on c4.

And after d takes c4, capturing on c4, we've achieved exactly what we set out to do — a long-term, permanent weakness on c4. Step three has two parts: complete development and solidify our own chain. The solidifying move every French-with-White player knows is c3. Not the knight to c3 — the knight goes to d2 here, because the ultimate plan is to harass and win the c4 pawn. I like to castle kingside first, getting the king clear with no nasty checks on b4, then play c3.
So we castle first — safe, since Black has no good way to hit d4; the rook to d8 is likely at this level — then we follow with c3.

Instead Black plays f6. Note the knight can't take on e5 — our f3-knight guards it. Black tries to open the centre, but that's counterproductive when you're behind in development. This is a great moment for flexibility: our whole c3-then-knight-d2 scheme is set aside, because f6 changes everything. Who benefits when the centre opens? The better-developed side with fewer weaknesses — clearly us.
So we welcome it — e takes f6, capturing on f6: you want to open the centre? Thank you very much.

Black recaptures with the knight, capturing on f6 — and now the e-file opens onto a massive weakness on e6. Two weaknesses in Black's camp: the new one on e6 and the old one on c4. Put them together and you get the classy move, the queen to e2, hitting both pawns at once. A good alternative is simply the rook to e1 — e6 is the juicy pawn; win it and we mate soon. After the queen to e2, though, there's the nasty knight takes d4: knight takes d4, knight takes d4, queen takes d4, we grab e6 with check, Black plays the bishop to e7, and I'm not sure White has a crystal-clear finish.

So the more controlled move is the rook to e1, leaving the queen guarding d4. It's incredibly hard for Black to defend e6, and Black's lack of development costs her — a developed f8-bishop would let her castle.
Black just doesn't have time to develop. The king to f7 tries to defend e6, but it's futile — the king is a poor defender in these positions.
There's a rip move — the simple fork on g5, knocking the king back. The game's far from over, though: we've won a pawn but our queenside is still undeveloped, so we need accuracy.

I'm expecting the king to g8, but our opponent plays fast and walks straight into the pin with the king to e7 — a terrible move. How do we punish it most clinically? The knight takes c6 is tempting, to set up a discovery, but it gives Black life.
The knight takes c6 lets the king slip via f7 back to g8. Better is to take on e6 with the rook, capturing on e6 — the check is a nice byproduct; what matters is the pin against the knight on c6.
The king to d7 — and now we can pre-move d5, ending the game: it wins the pinned knight on c6, and once that minor piece falls the king is hunted down.
So d5 is the game-winning move — we'll win without even using our back-rank knight or bishop, that's how powerful our existing pieces are.
The game's totally over — we take the knight next move, the knight can't move because the queen is pinned, and it's mate in three.

node.idea: This is the Advance French, chosen deliberately to practise closed positions — thriving in them is a genuine skill few players are comfortable with. The first job is the modest pawn to c3, building and bracing the pawn chain.

The way to understand a closed position is to zero in on what the battle revolves around — here it's the d-pawn at the head of the chain. Whoever controls that fight wins: hold it and you keep a big space advantage and easy development; lose it and the whole structure collapses.

Against the pressure on the chain comes an odd-looking rook-pawn move to a3 — and its purpose is to prepare b4, shoving the enemy pawn away and keeping the chain intact. Prophylaxis that also gains space.

Yes, it's two pawn moves and no piece development — but preserving the health of the pawn chain is exactly that important. And it isn't wasted: the queenside expansion also readies a further push to kick a knight, and opens the door to a fianchetto. Several gains from one plan.

Develop the bishop to d3 — and the square is chosen by seeing a tactic. It looks like the central pawn hangs, but it doesn't: after the exchanges a check springs in on the exposed diagonal, exploiting a standoff to win the queen. Always confirm the pawn is really loose before fearing for it.

Castle now — the pin-check resource is still available, so the pawn is safe. And notice the deeper point: don't develop the other bishop yet. Make the moves you know you must, wait for the opponent to reveal their plan, and only then place the discretionary pieces. That posturing over who commits first is a genuine grandmaster sub-battle.

asides.idea: The knight to f3 has an interesting history. Aaron Nimzowitsch — one of the patriarchs of modern positional chess, who wrote My System in the 1920s, originating over-protection, prophylaxis, and much of the vocabulary we now take for granted — faced the French often and played the knight to f3 religiously. It was first played back in 1826 by an unknown player; Nimzowitsch was maybe the seventh or eighth to play it, but he championed it.

This isn't the only French line where you give up the d-pawn — the Milner-Barry is another — but you must follow up very accurately or Black consolidates and we get nothing. White's best is the queen to a4, stopping the knight from coming to c5 and preparing to swing to g4. So the queen to g4, attacking g7 — Black can't castle, since that runs into the bishop to h6 winning the exchange, and if g6, we put the bishop on h6 anyway, with serious control of the dark squares. The bishop to f8 is a serious concession. Nothing happens fast here; White mounts a slow campaign, massaging the weak dark squares, getting the rooks in, a rook to e1 to overprotect e5. Moving the bishop back to e3 would be a tempo move, but I like the queen to f4 — b2 is hanging, but we're happy to sacrifice it; in these lines you must be ready to give up two or even three pawns to keep control, and the knight to g5, hitting f7, is a real threat. We keep the tension to get the queen to h6 and prevent castling. The queen to d8. Now a perfect chance to bring pieces in — the rook to c1 stops the knight to c5, confining it to d7, and controls the only open file; if the queen to e7, we infiltrate to c7. A cool idea against an opponent with all his pawns on one color: chip at the pawn shell with h4 and h5, since g6 is our primary target — if we play h5 and Black ignores it, we take on g6 with devastating effect. The knight to c5 — now tactics: calculate the h-pawn takes g6; if the bishop is taken, we have the pawn to g7 and then the queen to h7, forking the knight and rook, re-establishing material at worst. The queen to a3 heads into d6, the mouth of madness, and the queen to e7 is an elementary blunder — the rook to c7 wins the queen, with mate to follow. A nice technical game showing the power of this line; don't get tunnel vision on checkmate — you can use the king's weakness to win material — though here the rook takes c8 and the queen to d6 with check is mate in three.

node.idea: Because the fianchetto setup doesn't immediately challenge the centre, there's no need to rush e6. Instead — exactly as in the Caro-Kann — develop the bishop to f5 first, getting it outside the pawn chain before the e-pawn shuts it in.
Only now does e6 go in, with the light-squared bishop already breathing free air outside the chain. It's an ideal, harmonious structure — everything developed to its best square.
A useful little move — h6 grants the bishop a bolt-hole on h7, so that any lunge at it with a knight to h4 is rendered completely harmless before it ever happens.

The knight to c3 is a familiar inaccuracy at this level — it blocks the c-pawn's path to c4, its most natural challenge to the centre. That leaves the centre as solid as it gets, with the c5 lever held in reserve.
Now castle — and note there's no real threat to the centre: it's defended three times while attacked only twice. Counting the guards against the attackers is what tells you a threat is empty.
And there's the knight lunge — which is precisely why the little luft move went in earlier. The bishop simply steps to h7, unbothered.

The central break is a genuine idea, opening things up. The plainest reply is to swap everything off on e4, which strips away the fianchetto bishop and leaves the enemy king a touch draughty — but there's a sharper sequence worth finding.

The cleverness rests on the fact that the recapturing knight is itself loose. Snap on e4, and after the recapture an in-between capture on h4 wrecks the opponent's pawns while staying a pawn ahead. Order the captures right and the extra material comes with a ruined enemy structure.

There's no obligation to capture on e4 at all — allowing a rook to sit there, ready to swing across for a kingside lift, is unpleasant. Since the bishop isn't truly threatened, a calm recapture keeps everything sound.
The Zen move is the knight to c6 — the tempting pawn advance would just blunder the rook. Same central idea, but a developing move instead of a loosening one.

For the small price of doubled pawns comes an opposite-coloured-bishop middlegame — and those famously favour the attacker, because the defender's bishop can never guard the squares under fire. The knight recapture even forks a pair of pawns as a bonus.
Now the window: the opponent's bishop still isn't out, so the king is under-defended. There's a small chance to strike — pry the centre open at any cost and the lagging development gets punished.

f5 is more forcing than the quieter break — it drives the rook off its square. If it retreats along the file the centre push wins; if it captures, a knight recapture hits it back with a discovered check lurking behind. Every branch keeps a threat attached.
The point that makes it work: the enemy queen is undefended, so the pawn can't be taken. That single loose piece is what powers the whole combination.
And this is exactly why speed matters — the moment the bishop finally develops, the queen is guarded, the discovered attack evaporates, and the tactics are gone. Urgency is the whole idea.
No need for anything fancy — bring the last rook into the game and set up an x-ray against the queen. Quietly improving the idle piece is what converts.

The knight jumps to b3, hitting the rook in the corner. And a safety check first — scan whether the enemy queen can reach a square that hits g7 for a mate threat; it can't, so the plan is clean. Always confirm the opponent has no counter-mate before committing.

The finish looks like a slip — a couple of pieces hang — but sharp vision reveals a forced mate. It begins with the rook, not the queen: if the knight is taken, the queen crashes into e4 for checkmate. Trust the calculation over the material count.

tree.intro: Let's walk through Queen's Gambit vs King's Indian Defense — White plays the Queen's Gambit, Black answers with the King's Indian Defense. Watch how they meet.

It's a dangerous period — we're still quite undeveloped, our whole kingside is at home, so it's like we won a lottery ticket but we're in a war zone and need to escape before we can cash it in. Then the queen to d7 with check, and the king hunt begins — don't rush the first check you see, like the rook to f1 with check; map the king's escape, e8-d8-c7, and prevent it. Give a check on h8, the king goes to e7, and now every square is covered — the bishop covers e6, the pawn covers d6, the rook covers the eighth rank — and one more check is checkmate.

node.idea: d6 — we reach the first tabia, a big branching point almost every King's Indian passes through, with ten or fifteen viable lines from here.
The line I recommend — underrated, poorly studied, one most King's Indian players pass by — is the Averbakh, named after Yuri Averbakh, and it starts with the bishop to e2.

The bishop to g5 — not just development, but a prophylactic move.

The bishop to e3 — preserving pressure on the h6-pawn, with the queen to d2 to follow, and h6 as a hook for a pawn storm. It's not automatic to castle kingside in the King's Indian; keeping the king in the centre, which is so well protected, lets you storm with g4, h4 and g5 straight at Black's king.
The downside of the bishop to e3 is that e5 becomes possible — but it's not the end of the world, just a typical King's Indian move. Why the bishop to e3 for the semi-Averbakh —

because inducing h6 helps White; that pawn on h6 rather than h7 typically favors us. Now we close the centre with d5 — the whole point: closing it unties our hands for kingside action, since we no longer divert resources to hold the centre.

a5 — a typical King's Indian move preventing b4, usually followed by the knight maneuver to c5 via d7 or a6, pressuring e4. Another branching point; in the spirit of the Averbakh we go straight for Black's throat with a move that looks like a coffee-house move but is often the engine's top choice —
not h4, though that's possible, but directly g4.

because we protect e4 with f3. So we continue the kingside campaign with h4, launching the second pawn. Why not g5 immediately? That was also very good, I agree —

which sounds very hard, but there's a typical maneuver in these positions.

The idea is obvious: send the pawns at Black's king and open the h-file, using the h6-pawn as a hook — a pawn advanced past its start that acts like dynamite to blow open a file. Two things to mind: keep the e4-pawn protected — if Black's knight lands on c5 we play f3 to solidify e4, our main anchor; if the centre opens, the whole strategy collapses, so g4 and h4 depend entirely on keeping the centre closed. That's why, as Black, a common idea is to push c6, chipping at White's centre and preparing the queen to b6. Black can't fall asleep — the attack comes fast. Should we take the knight on c5? Almost never in the King's Indian: giving up the dark-squared bishop is a bad idea in maybe eighty percent of cases, because it lords over the position — controlling queenside squares, stopping the queen to b6 after c6, and above all supervising the pawn storm, controlling g5 and h6 and making h4 and g5 far stronger. It's a Swiss army knife; giving it up wrecks the dark squares, and after the d-pawn recaptures on c5 it hands Black the d6-square for the other knight.
