node.idea: f3 — one of my top recommendations for White, the Sämisch, named after Friedrich Sämisch, who developed a lot of systems connected with f3; the Nimzo-Indian f3 is also called the Sämisch. Against it, Black has a gazillion viable continuations.
Most lines start by castling; it's automatic. White generally plays the bishop to e3, though the knight to e2 also transposes. The point of f3 is twofold — first, to safeguard e4 —

and, in many cases, to prepare the kingside pawn storm with g4; the drawback is you can't use f3 for the knight, so the knight goes to e2. I want to play an old line I grew up on, played prolifically by Kasparov; nothing's inherently wrong with it — Black is worse only if White is incredibly accurate. Nowadays King's Indian players mostly play the Benoni with c5, considered objectively best, or the Panov —
the Panov with the knight to c6 and a6. But the old move is e5, the traditional way to play the King's Indian; a lot of people think you can't play e5 against the Sämisch — not true at all.
e5 is totally viable and frequently slips through the cracks; one drawback is that White has the pawn takes e5 —
which takes all the fun out of the game, but you've got to learn to play these types of positions too.
The queens come off on d8 — an endgame, a version of the Exchange Variation.

The knight to d5. I'll confess I'm not a specialist here — probably my first time. The knight takes d5 isn't forced: White recaptures with the c-pawn, and a pawn on d5 greatly hampers our queenside, controlling c6 and e6; the traditional treatment is the knight to c5, take, then c6 to remove the pawn, but the e2-knight slides to c3, and taking on d5 just replaces the pawn with a bloodthirsty knight. So the knight on d5 isn't that scary — it's attacking c7, which we must defend, and we can't play c6, since the knight jumps into c7 and traps the rook.

In the King's Indian, the queen's knight's traditional developing square is a6, so the knight to a6, protecting the pawn from the side. If the bishop to g5, we must play the rook to d6, getting out of the pin and protecting the f6-knight. Long-term, Black is favored: with pawns on c4 and e4, White has traded off d4 and accepted a gaping weakness there; most central squares are Black's, and once we get the knight off d5, we control d4, d3 and e3 — the whole central complex is weak, currently masked by that imposing d5-knight. Play c6 to chase it, get White to trade on f6, and Black is solidly better.

Our opponent is correctly taking his time. The bishop to g5, the rook to d6 — a very important resource, otherwise we lose an exchange. Note that sometimes giving up an exchange isn't the end of the world — the knight to c5 doesn't lose on the spot —

since after the bishop takes the rook, the knight can jump into e3; but it's all moot, because the rook to d6 is perfectly sufficient. This isn't just heading toward a draw — the resulting endgame is full of life and playable for a Black advantage; White isn't worse if very accurate, but most players relinquish the initiative and fall prey to the plan of grabbing the key central squares.
The knight to c3. The fundamental asymmetry: we haven't pushed our pawn to c5, which is why Black is positionally better.

c6 — we exploit the reserved possibility of pushing to c6, controlling d5; White can't exercise the same control over the mirrored square, d4, which is why White is often in a lot of trouble. The knight to e7 with check and the knight takes c8 is possible, but our c8-bishop isn't an integral piece — the heavy lifting is done by the a6-knight, which will head for d4 via the knight to c7 or c5 and e6.

We're not blindly closing our eyes and playing three moves — we'll do other things depending on our opponent. And from an opening-rules perspective, White has spent a gazillion moves with this knight.

He's taken the bishop and gotten the bishop pair, but his f1-bishop isn't impressive, just staring at the pawn. If White could push c5, that'd be a total game-changer. The knight to b4 has merit — probably our next move if permitted; if I play c5 we take with the knight, which is partly why we put the knight on a6, to prevent c5. White's best, and it's not easy, is the bishop from g5 to e3, restricting the a6-knight and preparing c5, which opens the f1-bishop —

because if we don't move the a6-knight away, it gets captured, ruining our structure, and getting the other knight to d4 becomes a cumbersome four-move process. Against all of White's ways to prepare c5, we have an important retreating move to prevent it. The bishop to e2 is the game continuation. The tempting knight to b4 is a bit of a dead end — after the rook to c1 we have the knight to d3 check, but we don't want to trade this knight unless for something on d4. Since White hasn't prepared c5, no rush. An interesting idea, though it fails concretely, is the knight from f6 to d7, covering c5 once more and opening the bishop to support a knight heading for d4.

Our king's knight was a little awkward where it stood, disrupting our coordination and needing babysitting, so the knight to d7 lends maximum energy to the knights — now both can access d4. A dream would be to trade the dark-squared bishops, making d4 ours forever, but it's not so easy; the bishop to f6 just encourages the bishop to e3, so don't assume your opponent makes the trades you want. And f5 isn't an idea here —

because when you consider f5, always ask who benefits from the position opening: generally not the side controlling the central squares. We want it closed, to single-mindedly focus on that square. g4 accomplishes little, actually weakening f4, so I'm already considering an arrangement with one knight toward f4 and the other toward d4, far in the future. My instinct is the knight to c5; the knight to b4 is significantly sexier now that our other knight is ready to support with the knight to c5, and it might be the most efficient path to d4, since after the rook to c1 the other knight jumps to c5, threatening a fork on d3 and using d3 as a transit point to f4, the square White just weakened.

There's one complication I can't quite make work, so maybe the mundane knight to c5 — but I'll follow my intuition; g4 can't be wrong. After the rook to c1, the knight to d3 with check — but knights are more valuable than bishops here, since the centre is closed; think of a knight as a Phillips screwdriver getting into the small spaces a bishop can't.
You're flossing the board a little. He can castle. The point of the knight to b4 isn't the fork — we're not expecting White to miss it — but to use b4 as a transit point toward f4.

Our opponent is disallowed d4. Let's proceed with the knight to c5, threatening a fork again, planning to drop back to e6 and finally get a knight to d4 — the first big step toward winning, though you can't win such positions in three moves; you do it step by step and celebrate the small victories.

What makes d4 important? It comes down to square control — a knight in the centre controls eight squares, a knight in the corner only two; a knight reaching d4 just lords over the whole position. The knight to d3 tempts, but after the rook to d1 we'd pin ourselves —

and we couldn't double rooks, since the bishop controls that square. So the knight back to e6, which comes with tempo, attacking the bishop, forcing it off g5, and making possible the future doubling of rooks on the d-file.

asides.idea: Skipping the knight to b4 would have kept the knight on a6 preventing c5, which opens another front. Why the knight to d4 and not f4? The queens are off, so no king attack, and the knight to f4 blunders to the bishop to c5, given our rook-and-king alignment — so I make a mental note to prevent the bishop to c5 whenever the knight leaves d4. Not b6, which is too slow and brittle, allowing a3 and b4; c5 isn't scary since it blunts the bishop and makes more weaknesses. The harmony in our pieces is great. He plays the rook to d1, and the knight takes a2 almost works — the bishop on e2 is a type-2 undefended piece on a forkable square, so the knight forks — but the bishop takes d4, and even taking the rook first fails, because the bishop to c5 double-attacks and the e2-bishop is still guarded by the c3-knight; White wins a piece. So instead we improve simply with the rook to d8, not c5, which would weaken d5, threatening the knight takes c2 to win the rook. White should move the king up to avoid the knight takes c2 with check. We prevent c5 with the retreating knight to a6 — not a failure, since we've installed a knight on d4; the b4-knight now assumes a defensive role preventing c5, and later heads for f4. The bishop on g7 could do more — to f6, with the idea of a check on h4 to disattach the king and enable the knight-takes-c2 tactics — so the bishop to f6 when the chance comes, though it's already supporting the knight. The bishop to f1 is innocuous. We head for f4 with the knight to c5, then, after b4, the knight to e6; if White plays c5, our rook drops back, and with the knight off a6, b4 and c5 are far less intimidating. An advanced endgame player induces as many weaknesses as possible first — the bishop to f6, though it allows g5, and White might follow g5 with f4 to undermine the d4-knight if the bishop leaves the long diagonal, so I flip-flop; ultimately the knight to c5, the original plan, get it to e6 and sink into f4, the second weak square g4 created. Would White draw with ideal defense? Absolutely, but tension accumulates and the clock dwindles — the art of converting a small advantage. The knight to c5, b4, and we don't play f6 and g5 to bury our own bishop; the bishop on g7 supports the knight, so we don't fear f4. Drop the knight back to e6 supporting d4, unafraid of c5, since the rook drops to d7. The bishop to f6 is even more appetizing now that g5 is stopped, with the idea of the bishop to g5 to trade the dark-squared bishop, White's main defensive piece. He plays b4; we don't care, we let c5 come and play the bishop to f6, shifting the front from the queenside to the centre and kingside. The knight to g3 — I commend the opponent. Our plan installs a knight on f4, but a much bigger achievement is to trade White's best piece, the bishop on e3, leaving him a bad light-squared bishop saddled by weak pawns; and if the bishop takes g5, the knight recaptures, still attacking the backward f3-pawn. This is the blunder: the d-file has been plugged by the d4-knight all game, but keep looking for tactics — we have doubled rooks and White's rook on d1 is defended only once, so the winning tactic is to take the bishop, lure the king onto a vulnerable spot, and play the knight from d4 to c2 with check; if the king goes to e2 to defend the rook, the knight to f4 with check finally lands and wins. The c2-knight controls e1, so the king has to leave the rook's defense — we win the exchange, then trade the other pair of rooks and use our rook to take all of White's second-rank pawns. Only twenty-eight moves. The simplest is the rook to d2 with check, trading a pair, then pick up pawns; the clinical move is, rather than grab the e2-knight, to dislodge the bishop with the rook to c2, and White loses the knight or the bishop, with the e5-pawn defending our knight.

tree.openingName: King's Pawn vs King's Indian Defense
tree.intro: Let's walk through King's Pawn vs King's Indian Defense — White plays the King's Pawn, Black answers with the King's Indian Defense. Watch how they meet.
tree.outro: That's how King's Pawn vs King's Indian Defense plays out.

node.idea: Against the Modern, we want a sound positional line rather than a sharp theoretical race.
We stake out the center with d4.
c3 is the quiet, strong choice: the pawns on c3, d4, and e4 lock into a chain so the fianchettoed g7-bishop bites on granite.
The bishop tucks into d3, where it defends the e4-pawn while the pawn chain looks after d4 — every unit covers the next.
We could play h3 to rule out a pin with Bg4, but Bg5 is the more aggressive continuation, provoking a decision.
With e5 the game sharpens — the idea is exd4 followed by g5 and g4, chasing the f3-knight off the defense of the d-pawn.
So we take on e5, keeping the h4-bishop passive rather than letting Black free it with the pawn break.
After the trades the question is the queen's-knight: Nd2 would drop the d3-bishop to Qxd3, so that square is off-limits.
Na3 looks ugly, but it's only a transit stop — the knight is bad on a3 for exactly one move, then it reroutes to its ideal square c4.
Nc4 leans on e5. You might ask why, since the queen guards the pawn — but pressure isn't only about winning material; it ties the defender down.

f4 is risky and does loosen our king, but the logic is clean: if Black takes, we push e5 and win the pinned f6-knight; if he plays g5, we take the knight with tempo on the queen. Even the Qc5-check has an answer — an interposition that hits the queen — which is exactly the resource f4 was counting on. Remember the three ways to meet a check: capture the checker, move the king, or block.

Now recapturing with the pawn is tempting because it hits the f6-knight, but a move isn't good just because it makes a threat: Black slides the knight to d7, and the e5-pawn, hit three times, simply falls.
So Nxe5 instead — it makes no threat, but it banks the extra pawn cleanly and keeps our structure sound.

Two ideas carry the position. First, sidestep the coming Rd8 pin with Qe2 before it lands — even at the cost of the usual 'defend with the least valuable piece' rule. Second, prepare slowly and attack fast: overprotect the centre first, and once Black's king is loose, look immediately for captures near it — that's how a shot like Nxf7 appears.

node.idea: The other side plays the Pirc — d6 and g6. It gets a bad rap for a simple reason: it hands us the full centre without a fight.

White's key strategy in the Pirc is to castle queenside and storm the kingside — you can't launch a pawn avalanche at the wing where your own king lives. So we clear the path for the king to c1 by lining the bishop and queen up on e3 and d2.

That battery has a bonus: the bishop can swing to h6 and forcibly trade off the fianchettoed bishop — Black's strongest piece, the one that supervises his whole defence. No need to rush the swap, though.
Now start the attack — h4. Take the hammer to Black's position; without ripping open files and avenues on the kingside, we never reach his king.
The knight jumps to h5, so g4 chases it out — we don't want it sitting there.
The whole aim is to pry open the h-file, the artery to the king. Rather than sac immediately, we play f3 to defend the g4-pawn — patience first, elimination later.

How to handle the centre? Since we're attacking on the wing, we want it closed — so d5 slams it shut. A closed centre buys the time to focus everything on the kingside; an open one splits your attention.
With the centre shut we transition straight back to the plan — h5, prising open the kingside.
He plays g5 to keep things closed, but the queen takes on g5 and it's simply winning — it threatens mate, and his only defence of the bishop drops the queen.
We recapture with the queen rather than the rook. The rook would have won a second piece, but keeping the queens on lets us keep taking the hammer to him.
He trades the dark-squared bishops to slow the attack, but we're still up a full piece.
Now, fresh blood — don't forget to finish developing. Castle, then reroute the knight toward f5 to lever open the g-file.
This is the maneuver: the knight to f5 either forces a trade that opens the g-file, or dislodges the queen — and then a rook lands on that file with crushing effect.
Even after a queen trade it doesn't matter — the attack has done its work and it's still mate in a couple of moves.

node.idea: The plan with black is solid, positional chess, and nothing is more solid than a Queen's-Gambit structure — meet the pawn on d4 with d5 and build from there.

White fianchettoes with g3, steering the bishop to the long diagonal. It isn't a dangerous line and there's nothing special to answer it with — the recipe is simply to develop the pieces to good squares.

Nf6 continues the plain development plan, guarding d5 and readying the rest of the army. Think of it as a war: pieces left on their home squares win nothing, they have to be marched to active posts before any attack is possible.
Bh3 offers to trade the fianchettoed bishop off, and it illustrates the whole drawback of that setup — the bishop leaves home only to swap itself, and the holes it was covering stay behind.
Accepting is right: taking the bishop hands White weak light squares around his king that the traded bishop was supposed to guard.
A very favorable swap. White has nothing in the centre and now an awkwardly placed knight on h3 — and note it well, that knight is undefended, so ideas that hit it become real resources later.
There's no reason not to stake a claim of our own with c5 — almost a Queen's Gambit with colors reversed, prodding the d4-pawn to declare itself.
Be3 is clumsy — it props up the centre pawn but ties the bishop to its defense, and White still isn't generating anything.
Taking on d4 would only help White centralize his bishop, so refuse the trade and develop the knight to c6, keeping the pressure and again inviting him to release the tension by taking on c5.
c3 shores up the centre but is another slow move — White keeps developing incoherently while our pieces flow out naturally.
e5 is available to prise the centre open, but the solid choice is e6 — keep the centre closed on purpose and outplay him in the quieter structure.
White takes on c5 — which was the real point of Be3, tying himself to that pawn.
Ng4 is the move: it hits the bishop and threatens to wreck White's structure, and its second point is that if the bishop steps away, we take on c5 and regain the pawn in fine shape.
White answers with Bg5. In these structures with a pawn on c5, White also has the pawn break b4 as a resource to remember.
f6 kicks the bishop and gains the crucial tempo. Never play f6 — except exactly when it comes with a threat like this.
The point of moving with tempo is that when the bishop is forced to shift, we can take on c5 immediately. e5 is tempting here but held back on purpose.

The drawback of e5 is that it would weaken the light squares f5 and e6 and undermine the d5-pawn — so in the name of solidity we take on c5 instead, keeping the centre firm and the light squares covered.
b4 attacks the bishop; keep it on the strong diagonal with Bb6 rather than let White chase it to a worse square.
Keep the knight near the centre with the reroute rather than the rim — linked knights are healthy, and from here the knight can later swing to c4.
By shoving the b-pawn White only manufactures weaknesses — his own pawn is now backward, and he's developing without any coherent plan while his position starts to crack.
Now think in terms of targets. White's knights sit miserably on the rim, and there are two clear plans — one on the queenside, one on the kingside.

The biggest queenside target is the pawn on c3, so rook to c8 takes the semi-open file. If he defends with a rook, that rook is nailed to the pawn — the weakness ties his pieces down, which matters more than the pawn itself, because he can't reallocate his forces while we can.
The kingside target is the h3-knight. A maneuver as old as the hills — bring the queen to h5 — gathers the pieces on that wing, attacks the knight, and builds real mating potential.

Qh5 completes the plan and White has essentially one move, Kg2, to prop up the knight. Look at the bishop on f4 — its retreat is blocked by the queen, and the knight on e5 eyes the c4 jump to hit the queen before a central break, though for now the knight on a3 is contesting that very c4 square.

node.idea: This is a worthy opening — either as your primary weapon or as a secondary one when you tire of e4. d4, d5, the knight to c3, and the knight to f6,

and the bishop to f4 — the Jobava London. A bit of history: the sequence first appears in the database in 1882 and is sometimes called the Mason variation; it was revived and developed heavily in the mid-2000s, and much of the modern understanding of the line comes from that work.

There are several replies here — a6; e6, the most common online; the bishop to f5, which our opponent played; c5; and e4, a sharp recent innovation, where before people played e3. The knight to c6 is one appeal of this line at a lower level, because after the knight to b5 White is not simply winning — that's a misconception — but you can win quickly if Black doesn't find the only way to stop the knight taking c7, which is e5, intercepting the diagonal; and here you're supposed to take with the bishop. node.idea: Against this gambit the cleanest reply is simply to accept — take the pawn and make the opponent prove the compensation they don't really have.

Here's a principle for disarming any gambit. Grabbing the second pawn is best by the engine's cold count — there just isn't enough compensation. But in practice the middle path is often wiser: hand the pawn back and, in return, claim a development lead. Stop worrying about clinging to the extra material and just get pieces out.

The developing move that also bites is the knight to c6 — it counterattacks the loose pawn. The natural-looking bishop development isn't as good as it seems, because a pawn thrust to d5 would kick the knight and hand over the e5 outpost.
Insisting on the sacrifice is just a bad decision — so capture on d4. The opponent's centre has caved in and they're simply shedding pawns for nothing; there's no reason to decline the gift.

The knight jump to b5 is pure intimidation — the sort of scary-looking move that concrete calculation keeps you safe from. Ask the obvious question: is there any reason not to just take the knight? The only pause is that the queens could come off and the king lose its castling — but two pawns up, with pieces trading, a king in the centre is a long way from getting mated.

This is a classic trap the opponent falls into — expecting an in-between check followed by a leisurely capture. What they've missed is that a single knight move to d6 does two jobs at once: it saves the knight and blocks the check. Two pawns and a piece to the good, the rest is technique.

Even deep in an endgame, the rule holds: keep developing, don't forget your pieces. So offer the trade of bishops — because when you're up material and a clean path to simplification appears, you take it. Every swap brings the win closer.
The plan is just e6 and the fianchetto — no need to overthink the technique. Grab the pawn back now that the knight has cleared away from its home square.
A touch of class: ask where the enemy knight wants to go — most likely g5 — and quietly deny it with h6. Not strictly necessary, but clinical, snuffing out counterplay before it starts.

A neat realisation about the winning method — the king isn't even needed here. Recognise that the bishop and lone pawn together can't force the issue by themselves, so the plan is to manufacture more.

Roll out a second passer with the kingside pawns, and now two connected passed pawns backed by the bishop are more than enough force to march one home to promotion. Connected passers plus a piece is overwhelming.
The one thing to avoid is the careless push to h2 — that would let the king plant itself in front and blockade the pawns by hand. Keep the king out of the blockade and the pawns keep rolling.
The precise route is to insert the bishop check on e3 first, and only then advance the pawn toward promotion. The check gains the tempo that clears the path cleanly.

node.idea: Against the queen's-pawn opening we play the Queen's Gambit Declined — the rite of passage for most improving players.

A neat move-order trick — sometimes lead with the bishop to e7. It quietly prevents an early pin, and if the opponent develops the knight, the reply keeps you out of the more annoying lines of the opening. Small orderings can dodge a lot of theory.

The cool treatment is a pawn to c6 and then repositioning the bishop from e7 across to d6. It looks like a waste of tempi, but it's the setup strong players favour — offering to trade the dark-squared bishops, which helps the defender, since that bishop is often awkward with no good parking spot.

You might object that no pieces are being developed — how can that be safe? It's all down to the state of the centre. With a solid pawn chain and a closed middle, the opponent can't break with the central push while their own king is stuck there, so you can afford several moves with one piece. Don't be a slave to the rule — judge the position intuitively.

A subtlety in the knight order — develop to d7 before f6, because leading with the other knight would invite a central leap into e5. Deny that outpost first, then bring the second knight out. And if the queen probes the b-pawn, defend with a rook: yes, the rook is tied to defence, but the queen is equally tied to the attack — a happy trade of duties.

Don't rush the central knight jump — but keep the key motif in mind: if it's exchanged, recapture with the pawn to pry open d5 for the other knight. Timing that break is what turns a solid position into an initiative.

Now is the perfect moment for the knight to e4, because after the exchange and pawn recapture the enemy knight can no longer retreat to its home square, and the piece stranded on the rim starts to find itself in real trouble.

There's a choice of approaches, and the positional one is to route a knight to d5 — a semi-outpost in the heart of the board. Resist the central break, which would only open lines for the opponent; keeping the centre closed is where the advantage lives.

What is the centralised knight actually doing? Nothing specific — and that's fine. It occupies a central square, radiates control across the board, prevents the opponent's pawn expansion, and stands ready to spring to f4. Think about what a piece does, but don't box yourself in by demanding a single concrete task.
As the opponent prepares to expand, the near-automatic response is a5, meeting the advance head-on and keeping the queenside from opening on the enemy's terms.

There's a way to prevent the pawn break for good — a pawn to a4, so that any advance is met by a capture that hangs a rook. No rush to play it, though, since the break isn't yet a threat; first swing a rook toward the kingside, and keep the freeze in reserve.

Pushing the enemy knight back takes real care — the immediate pawn thrust would only hand it a counter-outpost. So play the shielding pawn first to shut off that square, then the rook-pawn to chase the knight into the corner, and only then advance the f-pawn to blow the position open. One pawn stops the knight, the other does the pushing.

The traditional plan is to prepare the pawn break with a rook behind it. Toss in the queenside freeze first so the opponent gets no counterplay — there's never a formula for how much a wing pawn is worth, but denying counterchances before attacking is the safe order.

And the break lands at last — after all the patience, the knight that waited so long on its central square becomes the hero of the attack, and the pressure down the newly opened lines is about to make something collapse.

node.idea: The QGD has two ideas. First, a serious claim in the centre — the pawn on d5, solidly defended by the pawn on e6. Second, quick, effective kingside development without giving up our pieces' activity.
The bishop on e7 looks passive, but look carefully — it's the very piece that lets us expand our central claim, because it can support another pawn push.
That push, c5, creates central tension — complex, favouring neither side. This is what makes queen's-pawn openings a positional battle: the fight is in the centre, not a race to mate.
He plays the strong bishop to g5, pinning our knight — and the real meaning of that pin is that our d5-pawn loses one of its key defenders.
So we add a defender to d5 with the bishop to e6. Playing against a queen's-pawn opening you sometimes have to bite the bullet — a defensive move like this isn't passive weakness, it's sound.
Because our bishop now guards d5, he can't recapture there with the queen — only with the knight. He does, and that's a mistake: he never stops to weigh the consequences.
Here's the drawback — there's no need to take back the knight; we simply grab on b2 at once.
Now the theme: the queen is the worst defender of all. His queen on d1 is the only thing guarding the rook on a1, so we must drive it off that square.
The bishop check on b4 does it — practically mate but for the knight interposition, and after it his position is on the verge of collapse.
We take on d2, forcing the queen to move — recapture and we take the rook, decline and it's mate. A rock and a hard place.

node.idea: The pawn to e4, c6 — we're facing the Caro-Kann. How dare he play something I play with Black.
d4. Against the Caro, for a sharp line we could play the Nimzowitsch, but the classic sharp way —
the traditional, old-school way —
is the Panov Attack: we take on d5, the Exchange Caro, a gateway to very peaceful lines —
but the way to make it interesting and tactical, not to suggest the Exchange with the bishop to d3 isn't a great line —
is c4, immediately contesting the centre. You're trying to get rid of the d5-pawn, and developing with an eye toward pressuring it.
The knight to f6.
The knight to c3, pressuring the pawn.
He takes it, so he relents — and this leads to one of the most well-studied, most famous structures of all time, the IQP.
The bishop takes c4 — the Isolated Queen's Pawn structure. Why is it called that?

Because there's a pawn on d4 and it's isolated — no neighboring pawns, no c-pawn, no e-pawn; we gave both up. Whether the IQP is good or bad depends entirely on the circumstances — that's the magic; it can be the reason you win the game or the reason you lose it. But the bishop to f5 is a mistake — a classic fork, the queen to b3 forking two pawns, and we take one.

The queen to b3, the knight to d7, the queen to b5, e6. We shouldn't go crazy — this is where a lot of people go off a cliff with the knight to b5 and c7; we haven't completed our development, particularly the kingside. Instead of anything rash, let's complete development mindfully — the bishop to f4 prevents the rook to b8, though he's not really threatening it, because we're going to take the a7-pawn.
node.shortIdea: The queen to b3, the knight to d7, the queen to b5, e6.

asides.idea: We take the a7-pawn — careful the queen isn't trapped in a repetition as he chases it with the rook. He plays the rook to b4, hitting the bishop, which isn't scary at all: the bishop moves to b5, a great square protected by the knight, pinning his knight to his king while he's still undeveloped, and the rook on b4 is misplaced, so we threaten a3 to trap it. He plays the bishop to b8, and the queen to b7 is amazing because it pins the rook — a piece of higher value can x-ray a lower one, so if the rook goes to b3 it's undefended, and the knight takes with check exposes the attack on the rook. The queen takes d7 is bad, since the knight is defended by the other knight, and the bishop takes d7 would open the gates for his rook to come back — we want the gates closed. If he castles, we take his rook anyway. He plays the rook to b3, and the knight takes with check — check supersedes, we're not blundering the queen — and we take the rook; his queenside is gone. Now we castle and complete development. He builds a battery on h2, so rather than toy with it, we play g3 — weakening the light squares, yes, but we're up a rook and he has nothing on the kingside to do real damage — and it prepares the bishop to f4; the rule against pushing pawns in front of your king is overrated and needs moderation. The bishop to g4 attacks the knight, but instead of moving it we play the prepared bishop to f4, hitting his queen and getting our last piece out. Then we start trading everything on e5 — no more IQP; it's retired to the beaches. The bishop to f3 is delicate, because the queen to h3 would threaten mate on g2, so we deal with the bishop: the knight on b5 isn't really defending the king, so we drop it back to e2, heading to f4, which limits his queen to g4, and then h3 knocks the queen off its defense of the bishop. He takes, our king is perfectly safe, and we just push the pawn and win.

asides.idea: let's see when it was first played. Vasily Panov, born 1906, died 1973, was very obscure outside the Panov Caro-Kann; there was a Soviet 'black book' series annotating obscure players' best games by top grandmasters, and one was on Panov. But the opening itself was first played in 1844, long before Panov was born — as always, the person an opening is named after rarely invented it; Alekhine played it a million times. It's murky how these get named; maybe he wrote an article that went viral in the '50s.

node.idea: The pawn to f3 — the Fantasy Variation, my official recommendation: the most fun line against the Caro by a country mile.
Black takes on e4, giving up the centre.
We recapture on e4. Capturing there only makes sense in the context of one specific follow-up.

Against the pawn to e5 we don't take and don't play d5 — both allow the queen to h4 — instead the knight to f3, sacrificing d4 for quick development. But Black plays the knight to f6, a developing move that isn't the main line and invites e5, like a souped-up Alekhine. The knight to c3 would let Black revert with the pawn to e5, so we go the other way.
The pawn to e5 — if we mishandle this, the knight leaps to g4 threatening a fork on f2 and to win e5 back with interest, so e5 is near-automatic.

Black retreats the knight to d5. We've bitten off a big centre with only pawns, so the pawn to c4 is tempting but risky — pushing more pawns invites overextension. Still, c4 chases the annoying d5-knight, and Black's one central break is the pawn to c5; if we ever meet that with c3, the d5-knight becomes unassailable.
So the pawn to c4 — I flip-flopped, but it works, provided we follow up with accurate development.

Black retreats the knight to b6. The knight to b4 would be no danger — a3 chases it. And the pawn to c5 is simply met by d5, making our centre even more imposing while the c4-pawn stays protected by the bishop. This transposes toward the Four Pawns Alekhine, where you develop the queen's knight first — otherwise the bishop to g4 pins the king's knight.
So the knight to c3 — the most accurate, waiting for Black's bishop before committing the king's knight.
Black develops the bishop to f5 — exactly the cat-and-mouse we wanted, the bishop out first.
Now we can safely play the knight to f3.
Black plays the pawn to e6 — and still not threatening c5, because we always have d5 in response; that's why developing the knight to c3 promptly mattered.

The bishop to e2 — not d3, which would encourage the bishop to g4. Then we castle and bring the other bishop to e3 to solidify. The centre is our main industry; we check for the c5 break every single turn, since we need d5 to answer it — then the queen to d2, a rook to d1, even b3 Alekhine-style to reinforce c4.
Black develops the bishop to e7 — and it really does look like a Four Pawns Alekhine.
We castle — an inferior version of that Alekhine for Black.
Black castles. As White we have everything we could ask for.
We complete development with the bishop to e3 — the bishop to f4 was a viable alternative, but for now we overprotect d4, the linchpin of the whole structure, in Nimzowitsch's sense.

Black plays the pawn to a5, grabbing queenside space — but it loosens the b6-knight, so d5 gains appeal. We avoid a4, which would leave a hole on b4 for Black's knight; if the pawn reaches a3 we just play b3, a move we wanted anyway. So we keep improving flexibly and decide where the queen belongs.

The queen to e1 — heading for g3 and a kingside attack down the semi-open f-file. It allows c5, but Black is so poorly developed that the rook to d1 answers it, and d1 is a better home than the queen there, since the rook x-rays the black queen.
Black plays the knight to a6, rerouting — and we'll make that hard.
The pawn to a3 — no downside, and it locks the knight in place on a6.
Black plays the queen to c7. The c5 break is still serious, but after the rook to d1 we either push d5 or Black trades on d4 into a central massacre.
The rook to d1 — protect the centre before anything else.
Black plays the rook to d8. The c5 break still isn't a threat, because we can meet it with d5.

The queen to g3, completing the maneuver. Why is c5 and d5 bad for Black? The pawn travels to d6, forking the queen and bishop and trapping the e7-bishop. Players under 1800 struggle under strain, and Black is very cramped with a storm brewing on the kingside.

Black plays the rook to d7, preparing to double. Now the d6-square is a major weakness — it'd be a dream to plant a knight there, so we manoeuvre toward it with the knight to g5 or d2. The knight to g5 lets Black trade the important dark-squared bishop, but after the recapture we threaten the bishop to f6 and stop Black doubling.
So the knight to g5 — the more adventurous choice, packing a slightly bigger punch.
Black plays the rook to d8 — a lot of players would reflexively play h6 here. There's a juicy rook sacrifice available, but in time pressure we just complete the maneuver with the knight to e4.
The knight to e4, heading for d6. The knight to d6 looks like it drops a pawn, but at the end of the line the pawn to c5 forks the b6-knight and whatever sits on d6.
So the pawn to c5 first, establishing the stronghold before infiltrating d6 — and Black meets us head-on with the pawn to c5.

The tempting knight to f6 with check fails to the bishop taking f6 and the recapture, winning our queen, with a fork on d4 at the end. So instead the pawn to d5 — the move we've prepared all game. The point: the f5-bishop is loose, so if Black takes on d5, the rook takes f5.
Black plays the bishop takes e4, correctly — and we don't automatically recapture.

The pawn to d6 — a beautiful in-between move, shoving the pawn to fork the minor piece and the queen while the e4-bishop still hangs. It gets very dicey for Black; the bishop takes d6 is the only grandmaster-level try, meeting the recapture with the queen to c6.
Black finds the bishop takes d6. But after the queen to c6 we play the pawn takes e7, and Black can't recapture, because the d8-rook would hang with mate once the queen has left.
We recapture on d6. Black's defence is resilient, but we're winning anyway.
Black plays the rook takes d6 — the losing move.
Just the knight takes e4 — always look for hanging pieces first. The knight to b5 is even stronger, but I want my bishop.
Black plays the knight to c8. The downside is that Black gets three pawns for the piece, so conversion won't be trivial.
Let's play utilitarian — the knight captures on d6, taking the rook, the no-calculation move that ends the game.
Black plays the queen to e7. That knight on a6 was dead the entire game — the c5 break was a dead end with a pawn in the way.
The rook takes f7 — simple. It matters that our d1-rook is protected by the bishop; otherwise Black could take on f7 and then on d1 with check and recapture, winning material.

node.idea: We're Black, playing the Caro. c4 — the first time we see this move; White is clearly preparing to grab the d5-square as soon as possible.

But we still play d5 — very likely to transpose into the Panov Attack after the pawns trade and d4; White can also grab twice. Both variations likely lead to the same structure — the classic isolated queen's pawn.
The pawns trade on d5 — probably an IQP; the fact that he's thinking tells me he's maybe not too familiar with the Caro. Takes, takes, and e5.

e5 is definitely not the way, for many reasons — one is that it gives us an ideal French. We'd normally bring the bishop to f5 and then e6, but no rush; we could also develop the knight to c6. There's the idea of d4, to prevent White's d4 and sever the connection between the d- and e-pawns —
which also gives the bishop a nice square on c4, but let's not be too adventurous — the knight to c6 and the bishop to f5; no reason to refuse an ideal French setup handed to us like this.

The bishop to f5 — French players are completely in paradise: an Advanced French with the bishop on f5. One semi-drawback: in the French we'd have pawns fixed at c5 and c3, and here we've traded on d4 so the knight has a natural square on c3, but the bishop outside the pawn chain is no contest.
The knight to c3. Black has a very comfortable position — I don't think Black is better, it's still equal, but White is the one who has to be careful his pawn chain doesn't collapse.

Of course we play e6. Even with White’s pawn advanced to c3, there's also one advanced to c5 — they cancel; the presence of c5 and c3 doesn't make d4 any weaker or stronger, just one more attacker and defender, but Black holds the power, deciding when to take on d4, and White's queen's knight lacks the c3-square. g4 is interesting but not dangerous — we'd meet it with h5, and White overextends further.

The knight to f3 — he's a bit out of his depth, which is why the Caro or French can be effective at this level: not that they haven't seen it, just perhaps less well studied. Why not the knight to b4, threatening the knight to c2? Because the knight to b4 exposes the king to a check on b5 —

we don't want to bring the king up, so the queen to b6, just like in the French, putting significant pressure on the d4-pawn; the queen to a4 is the same concept, also forcing the knight back. Unlike the French, our bishop is on f5.

The one drawback, if you can call it that: we'll have to be creative developing the g8-knight, since in the French it often goes to f5, but the bishop is there. Two or three ways — the knight to h6, leaving room for the dark-squared bishop, then castle; or the knight to h6 or e7 and then a maneuver to vacate the f5-square for the knight. We'll do the bishop to g6 and the knight to f5.
I like starting with either e7 or the knight to h6. With the knight to h6, you should be curious why I'm not afraid of the bishop takes h6 — I hope he takes, so I can demonstrate.

As shown in my own game against a Peruvian grandmaster, it's not dangerous, because his dark-squared bishop is a very important defensive piece — without it the d4-pawn is much harder to defend and his position looser. The knight to a4 — fine; we can go the queen to a5 with check, but then the bishop to d2; the bishop to b4 with check looks good, but he just plays the bishop to d2, and trading dark-squared bishops isn't good for us.
It's good if he trades his dark-squared bishop for our knight, but I want to keep a bishop. No need for anything crazy — just drop the queen back to c7.
He castles.

a3, and the knight to f5 — everything is in perfect place; our knight has a home, our bishop has a home, all our pieces are developed except our king. We're going to castle —

and then embark on the middlegame. I have to compliment my opponent — he's handling this very well; not better for us, but a very comfortable position. Do we take on e3? No, for two reasons: that bishop isn't going anywhere, it'll be there for us to take later —

and why open the f-file for him, or eliminate a knight that's putting the d4-pawn under significant pressure? Instead let's begin by castling, the most flexible move. A very typical French idea follows —
the pressure has reached its apex; how do we take it to the next level? The move is f6.
f6, opening up the centre — there are some subtleties, but let's keep things simple.
The knight to b5, attacking the queen. Where should we go?

We can go to b8, that's okay, but I like dragging the queen back to b6 — it pins the knight to the pawn and reinforces the pressure on d4; after the pawns take on f6 and the bishop recaptures, look how many of our pieces will be trained on that d4-pawn, his position close to collapsing. If he doesn't take, we play a6, or remember we can still take the bishop and then the pawn — that's why we held off.

So we hold that over his head. A very funny subtlety I just realized: after a6 and the knight to c3, is the knight takes b2 possible? I missed this at first — after a6, the knight to c3, taking, there's the pattern the knight to a4, and the rook to b1 blunders the knight on c3 —

The knight on b5 is hanging — that's why it's so important to note all the undefended pieces; forgetting a piece hangs at the end of a line is one of the most common causes of miscalculation. Doesn't that give White an attack on the queen? No — the bishop is gone, and if White takes with the d-pawn, we take his bishop on e3 and his position collapses.

node.idea: Nc3 is the doorway to the anti-Sicilians — the Grand Prix with f4, the Closed with g3, or a transposition straight back into an Open Sicilian.
As Accelerated Dragon players we answer Nc6 — though a Najdorf player should avoid it here, since White can move-order you into a system you don't play.
The principled reply is Nd4 — the same motif you'd use against a Trompowsky bishop: the knight becomes a monster in the centre and hits the bishop at once.

We swap the knight for the bishop. Now a6 is the human instinct, but it's worth questioning your instincts — the b5-knight isn't dangerous on its own, so d6 or Nf6 hitting the loose e4-pawn are real options too.
Even after cxd4 this stays an anti-Sicilian — White has no light-squared bishop, so it's a different animal from a Najdorf. Our one problem is that we're badly behind in development.
Nf6 would run into e5, so we head that off — sometimes you accept a small positional concession rather than get crushed while undeveloped.
h6 stops Bg5 — the Smyslov idea of trading the knight and then planting one on d5. We have to keep a knight available to contest that square.
Now we finally develop with Nf6; if Bb6, Qd7 is a fine, if slightly awkward, answer, and the queen can reroute to c6 later to free the bishop.

Under pressure the queen must go to e6 — the only square that keeps e5 defended, since otherwise Nxe5 crashes in. Conducting an initiative cleanly is one of the hardest skills in chess, and it cuts both ways.

node.idea: He picks the Alapin, the quiet c3 move. Its whole idea is to build the big center with d4 next. Our job is to preempt that — don't let him roll his pawns to d4 and e4 unchallenged.
The tempting reply is e5, and it's playable — but pushing that pawn leaves the d5-square permanently soft. I'd rather not gift a hole on a central square, so we strike with d5 instead.
He answers e5 anyway, still angling to follow with d4 and grab space.
So we jam the door shut with d4 of our own, wedging a pawn into his position before he can get there first.
After the trade our pawn sits wedged deep in his half, cramping him and denying the natural central setup he wanted.
The bishop swings out to b5 to pin our knight. We've met this pin a hundred times — the only question is how we choose to break it.
We just quietly unpin with the bishop to d7. Not every piece needs to be doing something heroic — a modest developing move that solves the pin is plenty.
d3 here is a very typical mistake, and it's black to play and win. Two alarms should ring: first, loose pieces lie all around, and loose pieces drop off.

Second: the moment a pawn moves near the king, look at the diagonal it just opened. The check on a5 does both jobs at once — it rakes that fresh diagonal and forks the loose bishop, winning a piece outright, because our wedge pawn covers c3 so the knight can't block.
We scoop up the bishop. A whole piece to the good, and the game is essentially decided.
We grab the central pawn on d3 — though honestly we should have taken on b2, which would have snagged the rook in the corner too. I got greedy for the juicy pawn.
Here's the rule I hammer on: when you win a stack of material, don't forget to develop. Get your pieces out and coordinated instead of gorging on more pawns.
Now a lesson on converting. Trades are good when you're up material — but only take them when they fall in your lap. Never wreck your position just to force one.
His queen lands on d6 and it's actually trappable — Qc5 would hunt it — but there's something even cleaner.
The knight jumps to f5, hitting the queen and forcing the trade back on our terms. The extra material carries the game.
Into the endgame, and the same rules hold: consolidate first. We recapture and keep everything tidy.
The bishop redeploys to c6, its most active diagonal, doing real work rather than sitting home.
King to e7 — in the endgame the king is a fighter. No need to castle; walking it toward the center improves the coordination between our pieces.
Careful: dropping the bishop to b7 would run into a nasty rook check on c7. We sidestep to d7 instead, which also forces the rook trade.

Now the textbook conversion: pick a wing, make a passed pawn, and use the extra bishop to keep dislodging his blockading rook until it has to give way — then push the pawn home. And with a winning position, watch for stalemate before you finish.

We recapture on e4.

We recapture with the f-pawn, and Kusha responds with one of the most reputable lines against the Fantasy — the e5 variation; the point is that the d-pawn taking e5 runs into the queen to h4 with check.
So it's important to proceed with the knight to f3 — this is theory —

and the bishop to g4, the recommendation in quite a few books, incredibly solid. White has many reactions; the main move is the bishop to c4, threatening the bishop takes f7 and the knight takes e5. After it Black plays the knight to d7 to cover e5, White castles, Black plays the knight to f6. There's another move I analyzed — c3 — but what worries me is Black grabbing the pawn.
The bishop takes f3, the queen takes f3, the pawn takes d4, and I'm hunting for compensation. Let's play the bishop to c4 and stick to what I know is fine.
The knight to d7 — I'm definitely out of my league theory-wise here.
We should probably castle and keep developing.
The knight to f6 — this is the line. If White plays d5, Black responds with the bishop takes f3 and recaptures the pawn on e5.
So we support the d4-pawn, because Black is constantly threatening the pawn takes d4 — the move is c3.

The bishop to h5. Kusha knows this line very well; let's try to take him out of theory. We can play the bishop to g5 and then the knight to d2, or the knight to d2 immediately — but that blocks the c1-bishop, so I lean toward developing the bishop first. We can also play the queen to e1 to get out of the pin.

I like the queen to e1 — flexible, solidifying the centre, taking the sting out of the pawn takes d4. If Black develops the bishop to d6, a typical idea is the knight to h4 and f5, with the queen swinging to g3. The Fantasy is an attacking, tactical weapon — we want to play for the kingside attack.

I really like the queen to e1 — a dangerous move. The bishop takes f3 — a big move; Kusha gives up the important light-squared bishop, an integral defender, without which f7 becomes weak, and our bishop is now uncontested. How to recapture? Not a given — the g-pawn recapture solidifies e4, opens the g-file, and prepares f4 to knock out e5; a serious alternative, since Black hasn't finished kingside development.
But I'm not in an overly adventurous mood — I prefer the conventional rook takes f3.
The bishop to d6 — Kusha pre-moves it.

The bishop to g5, the queen to f2, and if the knight takes e4 we snap off f7 and the king is in huge trouble. This is a bit flimsy, but it's the Fantasy — and potentially very rewarding: with the centre, if we complete development we're better, but if the centre collapses we're in huge trouble.

The queen to c7 — I didn't expect it, but it's reasonable; maybe he wants to castle queenside. Why not the knight to d2? We must reckon with the pawn takes d4 and the bishop takes h2 with check — but that's a worthy pawn to sacrifice, since the pawn takes d4 is a massive concession giving us a juicy centre.
The knight to d2 is essentially a no-brainer — I'm more than willing to part with a corner pawn for full control of the centre. The rook to f8.

He's telegraphing queenside castling; the point of the rook to f8 is to defend f7. We can't prevent castling, but we can prepare. I have an idea combining tactics and positional play: the bishop from c4 to d3 — I know I said the bishop is crucial there, but circumstances have changed; f7 is no longer a weakness —

especially since Black is going to castle queenside, so protecting the centre matters more. The knight wants the c4-square more than the bishop; the knight to c4 comes with greater effect. After he castles and puts a rook on e8, our e4-pawn is nicely protected, freeing the knight for c4, pressuring the bishop and the e5-pawn; I'll happily take that bishop for two bishops against two knights. Pawn storms are slow, cumbersome, and generally overrated.
In opposite-side castling, a lot of people indiscriminately go b4, a4, b5 — that's not the only way.

You can also play with your pieces — the knight from d2 to c4. We're still sacrificing the h2-pawn; if he takes d4 and the bishop takes h2, nothing has changed — we'll still have a monster centre, and Black will have logistical problems getting the bishop back out.
The caveman attack has its time and place, but not every position. The rook to e8 — a great move. Let me think in silence.

The queen to g3 — its intention is to prevent the pawn takes d4. Didn't I want to encourage that? This is a dynamic position — things change every move: now the pawn takes d4 is an x-ray against my queen, with the knight takes c4 and f5 ideas, so it's a bigger enemy. The queen to g3 sits on a good square and stops the pawn takes d4, because the knight takes d6 wins the bishop with check. If the knight to h5, the queen tucks away on h3, x-raying the knight on d7. I'm starting to get control, though there's a lot of work to do.

The knight to g8. Notice the work of the bishop on d3 — a purely defensive piece, and defensive pieces are underrated: it guards the pawn on e4 so I needn't worry. Kusha probably wants f6 or f5. The tempting rook to f1 runs into f6, so maybe drop the bishop from g5.

The bishop to e3 — I like it a lot, because it solidifies the centre and attacks the g7-pawn. The bishop has done its job on g5; now it's time for a more defensive posture. Now g7 is hanging — that's our first threat.

g6 is a pretty significant weakness we can try to exploit later; Black's position is starting to show cracks. f5 isn't a threat — we can take the bishop, but no hurry, though maybe there is, or the bishop drops back to e7. One idea: the rook to f1 inducing f6, then take the bishop and reposition it to c4, or move the queen to h3, or launch the pawn storm — a4 is tempting, grabbing queenside space.
Let's start by doubling — the rook to f1 — and speed up a little; Kusha is a very fast player.

f6. I have an idea — the queen to h3, attacking h7 and x-raying the knight; the knight is protecting e5 and f6, so the queen to h3 strains those pawns, and that may lead to an unexpected tactic. I wanted the pawn to sit on f6 first, to restrict the knight.

Waiting moves and zugzwang do the rest.

He plays the Gurgenidze system, a cross between the Caro-Kann and the Modern, preparing to strike with d5.
There are many ways to meet it, but an underestimated one is to develop the bishop to c4 immediately — the point is to take d5 away from him.
And here's the common mistake: he props up d5 with e6, not noticing the very subtle reply that cements the weakness he's just created.
That reply is e5 — a move that permanently cements the dark-square weaknesses, straight out of a famous game that shaped how I see these positions.
He's forced to push d5, and we snap it off en passant.
Look at the wreckage: his bishop is passive, he's saddled with a weakness on d6, and he's dragged the queen out early instead of developing — a badly cramped position that's hard to untangle.
By jumping the knight to d5 he surrenders control of a gorgeous central square — so we slam our own knight into e4, eyeing the d6-hole.

node.idea: The reply c5 against the king's-pawn — the Sicilian. Today's choice is the Accelerated Dragon, a fast, clean setup and one of the friendliest gateways into the whole Sicilian family: less theory, clearly defined ideas, quick development.
White develops the king's knight to f3, the standard move against the Sicilian, eyeing the centre.
The queenside knight to c6 — the Accelerated move order. The plan from here is simple: trade in the centre, fianchetto, and get pieces out with tempo.
White strikes with the pawn to d4, the central break every Open Sicilian is built on.
We capture on d4, conceding a share of the centre for quick development and an open c-file to lean on later.
White recaptures with the knight, reaching the classic Open Sicilian structure.
Now the fianchetto — the pawn to g6, clearing the way for the bishop onto the long diagonal. Getting that bishop out fast is the whole point of the Accelerated.
Standard Accelerated Dragon theory — the fianchetto is set and Black is fully mobilized.
The move here is simply to castle and complete development before doing anything committal.
a5 is the point: it grabs queenside space and, more importantly, prepares a4.
a4 distracts one of the two pieces guarding e4 — and if the resulting trade favors us, we snap off the central e4-pawn in return for our flank pawn.
The main line runs into Nb5 and Bb6, hitting our queen and rook and handing White the initiative — but in exchange we've pocketed the central pawn, a fair trade.
d6 shores up the position; next we round up the offside knight with Nf6 and untangle.
First, move the rook out of the attack with Ra6 before anything else — safety before ambition.
After the trades, occupy the centre with d5, defend it with a rook, reinforce with e6, and reroute the c6-knight via a5 to the fine c4 square.

node.idea: Capturing on c6 is already a slight error — it opens the b-file for the second player and, just as usefully, clears the way to prepare the central break to d5. A trade that helps the defender is no trade to make.
The fianchettoed bishop must not be traded — resist by developing the knight to f6. And note the pawn move to e5 would be poor, since it hands over the d6 square as a lasting hole.
There it is again — that f-pawn move is one of the most weakening moves on the board, yet players toss it in reflexively. There's a good reason the old advice is simply never to play it.
The bishop out to c4 walks straight into the break you should be playing on autopilot — a pawn to d5, seizing the centre and opening lines while the opponent is still sorting out development.

The first order of business is to stop the opponent from castling and keep the king stranded in the centre — a queen to b6 does it. It may not prevent castling forever, but every tempo spent chasing the queen away is a tempo spent expanding in the centre, so even if the king eventually tucks away, it does so into a hot mess.

Expand — but with the right pawn. The natural central push would close the queen's diagonal and actually help the opponent castle. The move is e5 instead, keeping the diagonal live and the pressure on.

Now a crushing quiet move — a knight to g4. It's found by reading the opponent's intention: they want a bishop to e3 so they can finally castle. The knight leap stops that while feeding the attack, and the fianchettoed bishop rakes into b2. If the knight is challenged, a queen check on f2 leads to mate.

This is where intuition earns its keep. You don't need to see the exact mating sequence — one glance at the opponent's tangled pieces tells you it's there, and it's either checkmate or catastrophic material loss. Intuition is trusting that judgment instead of burning your whole clock trying to calculate it to the end.

Don't forget the other route — sometimes the simplest conversion is just to win a heap of material, a kind of insurance. If the attack ever misfires, you're still up a rook. When a full rook is on offer, take it, even if a mate might be lurking; the safe path is nothing to be ashamed of.

node.idea: White develops the queenside knight to c3, guarding e4 and looking toward d5.
The bishop settles on g7, aimed straight down the long diagonal at White's centre and queenside. Rapid, natural development is the accelerated dragon's calling card.
White develops the dark-squared bishop to e3, a natural square that supports the knight and readies queenside castling.
Our king's knight comes to f6, hitting e4 and finishing minor-piece development. Depending on White's next setup, we'll castle, play d6, or in some lines even strike with d5.
The bishop to c4 — a sharp Sozin-flavoured try that stares down f7. We simply carry on developing.
We castle, and note what we're deliberately NOT doing: pushing the pawn to d6 yet. Holding it back preserves maximum flexibility for what comes next.

The knight steps back to e2 — a poor choice, because it abandons the strong central d4-square and does nothing active. And here's a reflex worth burning in: whenever White keeps a bishop on e3, always keep one eye on it. There is a way to challenge White at once. We could play the calm d6 — perfectly fine — but if we want to be maximally testing, a sharper idea is waiting.
The knight jumps to g4, leaping at the bishop on e3. If the bishop moves, we get to hit f2 and b2 at the same time — and with the c-pawn already traded off, that double attack has real teeth.
White slides the bishop to g5 rather than the tempting retreat to d4, which would just drop the bishop. Now the second pattern to know is armed: the queen sortie.
The queen swings out to b6, forking the pawns on f2 and b2. It carries risk — our light-squared bishop still isn't out — but the pressure should tell.
White castles, choosing to hold f2 and let the other pawn go. A garden-variety double attack: one of the two pawns is going to fall.
We capture on b2. The key question before ever taking like this is always the same — can the queen be trapped? Here, no chance.

White chases with the rook to b1, and the queen simply steps to a3. That's the whole safety net: from b2 the queen had a3, and beyond it a5 and c5 — too many routes to be caught in a single move. That is exactly the check to run before snatching a pawn: list the queen's escapes, and ask whether any one move takes them all away.

White's best try — the knight leaps to d5, generating real pressure, so we must stay careful. Even so, it's hard to see much for the pawn; our position is solid. To consolidate we want the queen back — either to c5, or to d6. But the queen-to-d6 has to be calculated: it steps off the a3-e7 diagonal, dropping the guard on e7, and then the knight crashes in with a check on e7, forking the king and the knight on c6 — losing material. So d6 is out, and c5 is the safe route.

The knight comes back into the centre to e5 — retreating from a loose square, hitting the bishop, and centralising, all at once. And crucially the queen still guards e7 for now: if White probes with a rook to b3, the c5-square is always waiting for the queen.

White tucks the bishop back to b3, out of harm's way. Now we diagnose what's blocking full consolidation. We'd love to play d6 to free the light-squared bishop — but d6 cuts the queen's defence of e7 and drops that pawn. So d6 has to wait.

Instead we start kicking. Trying to fianchetto with b6 wouldn't cure the real disease — White's two strong pieces on d5 and g5. We need to chase at least one away, maybe both later with a well-timed e6. The pawn to h6 first — the most flexible poke, keeping options open depending on where the bishop runs.
The bishop retreats to h4, staying on the pin — and where it lands decides our next step.
We keep coming — the pawn to g5, chasing the bishop away entirely. This unburdens our position and lets us consolidate on our own terms.

The bishop drops to g3. Now d6 finally works — e7 is covered well enough. We could also try e6, but combining g6 and e6 leaves too many dark-square holes, so there's no rush to chase the d5-knight yet.

So the pawn to d6 at last — solid and freeing. And if White tries the knight to c7, there's simply no follow-up: the rook steps to b8 and nothing comes of it. That jump only bites if a rook were sitting on e8, which it isn't.
White plays the correct plan — the pawn to h4, prying open our king. This won't be an easy game.
We finally develop the light-squared bishop to g4. Honest admission: White's h4 is stronger than it first looks — this was underestimated.
White centralises the queen to d2 — a good move. Now we've got an interesting resource: the queen to a5, trying to force the queens off.

The queen to a5, offering the trade. There's a tactical wrinkle — White has the check on e7 — but calculate one step further: after the knight takes e7 with check, the king steps to h7, and now we hit two things at once, White's queen and the checking knight, so the queens come off. We hand back the extra pawn, but the mating danger evaporates.
White declines and lifts the queen to e3 — music to the ears, because now the check on e7 no longer bites: that knight is tied to defending White's own queen, so the moment it moves, the queen falls.
So the queen to c5, again pressing for the exchange and eyeing White's queen.
White sidesteps to d2. No matter — our queen is beautifully centralised while White's is tied to the knight. That means we can get on with the plan: e6.
The pawn to e6, kicking the d5-knight. A strange, tense structure — the pawn-grab has led to a real fight, and if the knight retreats to e3 there's a very pretty resource waiting.
The knight goes to e3. And here's that resource — not a gimmick, it genuinely does something.

The bishop drops in to f3! It's untouchable thanks to the fork, and the point is plain: we're hitting the e4-pawn. With such a strong knight on e5 backing the operation, that pawn is hard to hold — normally a capture on c5 would break the pin, but the other knight just recaptures and the bishop stays immune.
White grabs on g5.
We have to recapture on g5 — otherwise our whole kingside is shattered.
White captures our centralised knight, the bishop landing on e5.
We recapture on e5 with the other knight — all according to plan.
The knight to g3, a good defensive try. Suddenly our f3-bishop could become a liability — if White's queen ever steps aside, the bishop can be taken. Time to think about shoring it up.

The pawn to g4 — solidifying the bishop, and more than that, preparing to sacrifice it: if White captures on f3, our knight recaptures and gets anchored by this very pawn. The deeper idea is to bring the dark-squared bishop to h6 and crank up the pressure.
White finds a very strong move — the queen to c1. And now our f3-bishop really is trapped.
We carry on with the plan — the bishop to h6, pinning the knight and pouring heat onto White's position. The f3-bishop is lost, so we roll with it and turn it into fuel.
White takes the bishop, a pawn recapturing on f3.

And now the instructive choice — most players would recapture with the knight, but we take with the pawn. This f3-pawn is a far more dangerous attacker: it jams White's position and becomes an anchor point for mating ideas. We're down a piece for two pawns, but White's king is the one in danger.
White unpins with the queen to e1. We have many ways to improve.
The king to h7 — stepping off the g-file so the rook can pour down it into the attack.

White cracks under the pressure — the knight to c4, which simply hangs itself. But the beautiful point is that we don't need to take it. The first thing to notice isn't the loose knight — it's that White's pawn on f2 is now pinned, so it no longer guards the knight.
So the in-between move — the rook to g8, threatening the crushing capture on g3 with check. Once that knight vanishes, White's king stands utterly alone.
White's king shuffles to h2. We keep our eyes on the bigger prize, not the loose knight on c4.
The knight to g4 with check — crushing.

The king to h3. Now don't drown in the sea of winning moves — plan properly. The real target is getting the queen over to the kingside, ideally to h6. What's in the way? Our own bishop. So move the bishop first.
But we don't bury the bishop uselessly — the bishop to f4 keeps it in the attack while clearing the queen's route via g5 to h6.

node.idea: Through a strange move order we've reached a Jobava London, and the whole game turns on one idea: trading the dark bishops to expose White's centre.

The key operation: meet the dark-bishop sortie with Bxh6, deflecting the queen away from the pawn on d4. It looks like it wrecks our castling, but the point is the centre — once we hit d4 with c5, the whole structure starts to buckle.

node.idea: We have the Black pieces against a good player. As promised, I'm going into my main repertoire. d4, the knight to f6.
The Jobava London — the queen's pawn paired with an early knight to c3 and the bishop bound for f4, a sharp, tricky setup.
The knight to c3 is the introductory move; I'll oblige with d5, and this is going to be a very interesting twist.

Of course the bishop to f4 isn't the only move, and we are indeed facing the Jobava London — I'm now Black against my own opening, but I won't hold back, I'll give my honest recommendations. What you should understand about the Black side of the Jobava is that there are seven or eight equalising lines — it's impossible to say that e6 is worse than the bishop to f5, or a6 worse than e6; all the typical moves here, other than the knight to c6, which blunders the knight to b5, are approximately equivalent in objective strength. 'Best' is relative — each line leads to a different type of position, and whichever you play, you have to know it well, because almost every move is good. Even the relatively rare c6 is quite decent. The move that's probably easiest for most people to understand, because it's also the most forcing —
and you could call it the most principled — is the direct central strike, c5. You're basically trying to punish White directly for bringing the knight out to c3.

The queen is driven to a5, and we can probe again — a maneuver that repeats and, at the right moment, wins the queen outright.

One general warning this line teaches: never lean on a pin alone to keep your queen safe. If the pinning piece can be distracted, the queen is hanging the instant it happens, and you bleed tempi trying to save it.

After the queens come off, don't rush — develop with tempo. Castling long with check is the classic device, gaining a free move while the king tucks away and leaving a full, healthy extra pawn for the endgame.

node.idea: This is the Jobava London — the knight to c3 paired with the bishop on f4. It looks innocuous, hardly an attacking weapon, but that's an illusion: it's a genuinely aggressive system, and players who underestimate its potential get burned.

The pawn to c5 is already a slip. It tries to punish the early knight development — in a normal London you'd prop the centre with a pawn — but committing the knight to c3 has a hidden virtue: it puts immediate pressure on the d5 pawn, which changes everything.

Because of that pressure, a capture on c5 becomes available — a move you'd never make in the traditional London. It intensifies the heat on d5 and makes winning the pawn back surprisingly awkward for the opponent without falling behind.

The natural knight development is the common online choice but it's wrong here — the accurate move is the rook-pawn to a3, with the obvious idea of following up with b4 to cement the extra pawn on c5. Preparation before consolidation.

The opponent grabs the centre and eyes winning the pawn back with interest — but there's a catch. Instead of meekly retreating the bishop, plant it on g5, and the power of the early knight shines: now there's a threat to swap on f6 and capture on d5, knocking out a key central pawn while keeping the extra material.
The opponent has to waste a tempo defending, which is exactly the opening to secure the c5 pawn with b4 — the whole reason the rook-pawn went to a3 earlier. A full pawn up, and for no compensation.

Develop modestly to e2, not the more natural square, which would walk into a fork. And appreciate the extra pawn — it's not just any pawn; sitting on e3 it's a speed bump, restricting the opponent's central break and choking the squares their pieces want.

The queen shift to e8 is tricky — it lays a trap. Snatch on d5 too soon and the alignment of the opponent's bishop with the rook in the corner springs a discovered attack on the knight, winning the pawn back with interest. Just stay up the pawn and don't take the bait.

And a genuine surprise — a knight leap to e4 that's easy to miss. It forces a sequence leaving one side with a rook and two pawns against two minor pieces, a fascinating material imbalance to navigate.
node.shortIdea: And a genuine surprise — a knight leap to e4 that's easy to miss.

asides.idea: A useful rule of thumb in these imbalances: with two rooks against two minor pieces, trading a pair of rooks favours the side with the rook — and in pure rook-versus-two-pieces endings, with nothing else on the board, the rook often dominates outright.

node.idea: Which system to use against the London depends entirely on what you already play against the two main queenside openings — a Queen's Gambit player answers with the central pawn, a King's Indian or Grünfeld player fianchettoes, a Benoni player strikes with the c-pawn. Reach for the setup you already know, and the least flexible choice is the passive one.

The move that really challenges the London is c5 — it lets the opponent capture, which is ambitious and mainstream, and immediately contests the centre, essentially playing it like a Queen's Gambit a move down. Confrontation, not accommodation.

The bishop out to b5 is slightly offbeat — normally the c-pawn goes first in the London. And here's a deep positional idea: a queen check to a5 doesn't win the bishop, but at this level you play moves that induce a move you want. The whole London rests on d4 being a fortress, and it's rock-solid only once c3 supports it.

So the check induces a knight to c3, which permanently denies the c-pawn that support — and d4 flips from a strength into a weakness. As a bonus the queen stands beautifully active, and there's nothing wrong with leaning on the bishop while you're at it.

Stay active — e6 now would be too passive with development lagging, inviting a central knight leap. The move is a bishop to g4, pinning the knight that props up d4 while developing a piece. Restrain and develop in one stroke.
The bishops come off, and the recapture toward the centre leaves a compact, healthy pawn structure — the kind of solid shell that's a pleasure to play from.

There's a choice of resolving the centre now or playing e6 first — and the guiding rule when unsure is keep the tension. Let the opponent be the one to decide whether to capture; carrying that question is always more of a headache for them than for you.

Take on the knight, or retreat the bishop? The deciding question is whether the opponent would realistically lash out with a weakening kingside pawn push — and the answer is no, there's no reason to fear it. So hold the tension and drop the bishop back.

That pawn thrust weakens the shelter in front of the king. The central knight jump looks intimidating but it's surface-level — it merely hits the loose pawn, which just needs careful defending, sidestepping the tempting queen move that runs into a knight fork.

Now a principle to bank — the rule of piece value: carry out any task with the least valuable piece that can do it. So a rook drops back to defend the pawn. It isn't glamorous, but pieces have to do the dirty work sometimes, and there's nothing wrong with that.

Now it's time to take stock — keep the king in the centre for the moment, and set the priority: to make the open h-file pay, the defending bishop has to be eliminated so the advanced pawn behind it loses its guard.

The obvious knight jump fails to concrete calculation — a trade sequence leaves a pawn hanging with a fork and the queen crashing in. But failing on one move doesn't kill the plan; it only rules out that one route.

So modify rather than abandon — the knight to h5 instead. It temporarily clogs the h-file, but piece placement is temporary while the long-term priority of prying that file open is permanent. Don't confuse a short-term blemish with a real problem.

The knight loops back around, and now the advanced enemy pawn simply can't be held. Distinguishing the temporary from the permanent is the whole art here — you can't make an omelette without cracking a few eggs.
Double the rooks and never surrender the file — a pawn to the good, heavy pressure down the h-file, and every positional trump. Now it's just a matter of precise conversion.
The queens and a pair of rooks come off into a knight endgame a clean pawn up — and now the plan is to open a second front, rolling the queenside pawns forward starting with a5.

A move that looks dreadful — b3, deliberately closing the position — but its purpose is to fix the weakness so it can be targeted. Locking the pawn in place is what makes it a permanent target rather than a runner.

And the point is revealed: the opponent can't stop the knight from reaching d3, and with the weakness now fixed it can't be defended either. One quiet preparatory move set up the decisive infiltration.

The queen swings to b6, pressing the pawn and setting up the tension between the queens. This is the move that leads to a structure many opponents in this range struggle to handle.

Should you trade the queens? No — that would let the opponent recapture with a pawn, and the resulting semi-open file matters enormously; you want to be the side controlling it. So instead encourage the trade on your own terms with the pawn to c4.

The typical plan hinges on a detail — the enemy rook in the corner is undefended, so there's a standoff between the rooks. Exploit it to steamroll the queenside with b5, which also supports the advanced c-pawn and threatens to break through, the follow-up knight capture being untouchable because taking it would drop the hanging rook.

tree.intro: Let's walk through London System vs Caro-Kann Defense — White plays the London System, Black answers with the Caro-Kann Defense. Watch how they meet.
