node.idea: White opens d4, and we play the King's Indian move-order, the knight to f6.
The knight to f3.
We fianchetto with g6, heading for a King's Indian — my real opening repertoire at this stage.
The knight to c3 — the entry to the Jobava London or Barry system.
We play d5 here to stop White from move-ordering us into a Pirc, which we're not playing in top-level play.
The bishop to f4, and we've transposed into the Jobava London — the old name is the Barry system, specifically the setup against g6.
We complete our fianchetto, the bishop to g7 — all standard fare.
White plays e3.
We complete kingside development with castling.

White plays the bishop to e2 — a quieter, tamer, more positional treatment. There's a sharp, tactical way to play the Jobava London, connected with an early pawn push, but here White is playing it strategically and quietly.
Black has a million ways to disarm the Barry. I'll play solidly — starting with c6, shoring up the centre and in some lines preparing the queen to b6.
And White does play h4, combining two ideas: the bishop to e2 lulled us into a false sense of security, and now suddenly the h4 attack.
Very dangerous. The typical response is h5, stopping White's h-pawn.
The knight to e5, in some lines preparing a quick g4.

We have to get this knight off the board ASAP, so the knight to d7 is standard — otherwise White plays g4 and crashes through, and we could get mated. If White plays g4, my plan is the knight takes e5, d takes e5, the knight takes g4 — in time to eliminate the g-pawn while keeping the kingside intact.

Jobava players like to keep the tension with a move like the queen to d2. Once White plays h4, it's clear that in almost every case White castles queenside — so we're heading for an opposite-side-castling position with attacks on both wings. f3 is a very good move, preparing g4; our opponent is showing fantastic knowledge of the system's ideas.
We could play the queen to b6 hitting b2, or the queen to a5, but I'll implement a creative idea — we take on e5, capturing on e5.
White recaptures, capturing on e5. One drawback of f3 is that it weakens e3 — that pawn is now a target.

I'll play the unconventional bishop to h6 — within the framework of attacking the weak e3 pawn it makes sense. Players find it awkward to move the bishop off its fianchetto spot, but here it works, especially because if White pushes e4, he'll struggle to castle queenside, since our bishop will be holding c1. So e4 is way over-ambitious.
If White plays the queen to d2 — the standard defence of the pawn — then our bishop exerts nasty long-term pressure on this diagonal. Now we prepare for White most likely castling queenside next.

If White castles queenside, we'd want a queenside attack — so preemptively, b5 might discourage it. It's like a lead-off in baseball, stepping off the base ready for the pitch. If White doesn't castle queenside, b5 costs nothing and grabs space; if White does, we've gained a tempo, our attack already started. And every tempo is crucial in opposite-side castling, since White will try to get g4 going.

White takes their time with the bishop to d3, a nice move — I assume preparing to meet things with the knight to e2, a high-level idea. Our options: drop the knight back to d7 to trade off that annoying bishop; or something tactical like c5 for pandemonium; or b4, the knight to e2, then c5, staking a big central claim; or the knight to d7, the bishop to f4, the bishop to g7 to prepare e5.
The knight-d7, bishop-f4 trade looks sterile, so let's go crazy — b4, chasing the knight and forcing a decision.
The knight to e2.
And the follow-up, c5.
Why start with b4? First, to expand on the queenside; second, we were threatening c4, which would trap the bishop. White plays c3.
White's treating this like a London. We take, capturing on c3, to fully discourage White from castling queenside.
White recaptures, capturing on c3. We've opened the queenside and prevented queenside castling, which would now be madness with the b-file open — very easy to reach White's king.
Now the second idea — the knight back to d7 — to open the centre. Why? Because White's king is stuck in the middle.
White can castle kingside, but then the h4 pawn becomes a major liability; queenside castling is easy to punish; and if White stays in the centre and we open it, we get to the king.
So we drop the bishop back to its fianchetto square, g7, preparing e5 — which would blast open the centre and open the bishop's diagonal, with very positive consequences.

The rook to d1 — clearly our opponent sees the idea and discourages e5. Do we push anyway? If e5, d takes e5, knight takes e5, there's the weird bishop-e4, and our d5 pawn crumbles a bit — so maybe prepare one more move.
We play the bishop to b7 — which seems silly in isolation, biting on granite, but after e5 and the trade it makes sure the d5 pawn isn't a soft target for White's heavy pieces on the d-file.
g4 — now things really heat up, and I'll likely go quiet as it gets tactical. After take, take on h5, we push e5, feeling good for Black.
We take, capturing on g4 — starting with e5 first would allow g takes h5, which feels scary and could get us mated, so this order first.
White recaptures, capturing on g4. I'm not ruling out getting mated, but with accurate play I hope not.
Now e5, opening the centre and striking at White's well-protected d4 pawn — things really heat up.
The bishop to g3. Time's fine — four minutes, plenty. We force another decision.
We could snap off a pawn, but I go with my gut — the rook to e8, keeping the tension and preparing e takes d4, putting the rook in an x-ray with the king.
White castles kingside, abandoning the mating ambitions for king safety — probably the right call. I underestimated that move.
The knight to f6 — actually the immediate knight to f6 is a smart alternative, with tactics behind it I'll explain after the game.
g5 — most people eye the bishop takes e5. What if White just snaps the pawn? The knight to g4 or the knight to h5 make sense.
Let's go knight to g4, going after the e3 pawn. Maybe the knight to h5 and the queen to d7 was better, but too late now.
The knight to g4 is probably a mistake, but not so bad. White plays the bishop to b5.
We could take on d4, but why not calmly bring the rook up to e7, also solidifying the very valuable f7 pawn?
White takes the pawn, capturing on c5. Now we'd love to win it back.

We can win it back with the queen — the queen to c8 makes most sense, with more tactics behind it: if White pushes c6, after the trade White can't take on d5, because we'd pick up the e3 pawn with a fork. That's why I didn't play the rook to c8.

White pushes c6, we take with the queen, White takes with the bishop, and we recapture, capturing on c6 with the bishop — and once we collect the c5 pawn we'll have an intact centre, excellent coordination with both bishops fianchettoed, and White's pawns terribly weak.
White plays c6 and the bishop to f2 — but we're very close to winning; he wants to take on d5.

Let's solidify — the rook to d8, protecting d5 and bringing the rook into play. I expect e4, then we double on the d-file and blast through the centre. Black is borderline winning, strategically, given how many weaknesses White has.
The knight to g3. If I keep my clock under control, we're going to win.
e4 — not sure it's best, but it opens our bishop and creates strongholds for our knight, which can circle back to e5.
The rook to c1.
The knight to e5 — very juicy squares, and the queen can drive in on the light squares too.
White's starting to crumble. The knight to f3 — an outpost, also hitting the h4 pawn.
White plays the queen to e2.
We capture, taking on h4 with check — not just for the free pawn, but because now the g5 pawn is a huge weakness.
The king to h3 — and I see a mating net forming around it.
We don't need the complications — we simply go back to f3.
The rook to h1 — I'm not worried about anything on the h-file; there's no attack.

And there it is — the Maróczy Bind, the very thing most people who avoid the Accelerated Dragon are afraid of, and rightly so. It's both a variation and a structure: pawns planted on e4 and c4, both trained on the d5 square. That's the bind — it makes the freeing break to d5, the whole point of the Dragon, virtually impossible, leaving black cramped.

Here's the dangerous, under-the-radar answer: instead of the automatic fianchetto, start with the knight to f6, delaying the bishop. It immediately puts the question to the e4-pawn and hands black real chances to fight for the initiative rather than just sit passively.

A tactical footnote that makes it sound: if the opponent captures on c6 and pushes to e5 to boot the knight, there's a queen check on a5 that scoops the e-pawn back. The whole idea holds together on concrete tactics.

Now the step that startles the uninitiated — capture on d4, dragging the queen out into the centre. It looks reckless, inviting the knight to be pinned with a menacing central push, but it works out concretely for black.

It's important not to fianchetto here, since that would walk into the central push — so insert d6 instead. It frees the bishop and, just as importantly, jams the advance of the enemy e-pawn. If it pushes anyway, it's simply captured; and even if the queens come off at the cost of castling rights, that trade isn't worth a whole pawn to the opponent.

Here's the whole reason the Caro exists: unlike the French, we get to develop this light-squared bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain, to f5, before we ever shut it in with e6 — and that's exactly what we've done. White answers with f4, grabbing more central space, but it's not a good move: it curbs the development of White's own light bishop and it weakens his king.
The proper reply is e6 — White has over-committed his pawns while lagging in development.

White develops the bishop to d3. Since this is our first Advance Caro, here's the rationale. The centre is CLOSED, and a closed centre is built of pawn chains — our black pawns form one chain, and d4 with e5 is White's chain. The side with more levers, more ability to attack and undermine the OTHER side's chain, is the side holding the initiative — and the whole point of the Caro is that Black is that side. White's compensation is space; those two things balance out. And right now we don't want to surrender this prime parking spot on f5 so easily — we trade it on OUR terms.
Trading on our own terms means: when this bishop comes off, we want to replace it with a KNIGHT. So the typical move is the knight to h6 — and if White takes on f5, we recapture with the knight.
White develops the knight to f3. Why do we want our knight to reach f5? To pressure d4. So the question becomes how we keep piling onto that pawn.
We play c5 — hitting the base of White's pawn chain, and at the same time opening the c6 square for our knight.
White trades, capturing on f5.
We recapture with the knight, capturing on f5 — and now we have TWO attackers bearing on the d4 pawn.
White castles. Now we could grab d4 at once, but to play it cleanly there's a subtlety worth a second — and note White can also take on c5, which we'll deal with.

Rather than snatch d4 immediately, we play the knight to c6 first — the more flexible move, since we want it on the board regardless. The queen to b6 is also possible, but we hold it in reserve: if White plays c3, THEN the queen to b6 becomes strong.
White plays c3, showing his intent to prop up d4.

Now the clean way is to take on d4 first and then play the queen to b6, winning the pawn — and in a real game that's what I'd do. But I want to show a beautiful idea, so I play the queen to b6 first, hoping he grabs a pawn.
White plays b3, refusing to walk into it.
He won't allow the trick, so we simply take, capturing on d4 — there's a lot to unpack in this Advance.

White recaptures, capturing on d4. This is a critical pawn: it's the link that breaks up his chain, and with two of our pieces attacking it against a single defender, it's falling — and his whole position starts to crumble.
The knight from c6 takes, capturing on d4 — we've won the pawn and reached the decisive stage: up material, with a protected passed pawn on d5.
White plays the king to h1 — a good move, sidestepping a discovered-check threat.
We ask what we haven't done yet, and develop with the bishop to c5 — a great move. The h5 push was also good, but we save it; g4 would have been White's best, though I don't expect it.
White takes our knight, capturing on d4 — a mistake; now he collapses. The only question is what we recapture with.
We recapture with the bishop, capturing on d4 — the right choice. White's rook is now in trouble, and the game is essentially over: he's losing it.

White finds g4. Here's a common trap — tunnel vision. After a move like the bishop to d4, many players automatically snatch the rook on a1. But look wider: taking on a1 gives up our knight, so White gets a knight back for the rook — a real chunk of material. So we do NOT grab the rook immediately.

And not the knight to e3 either — White just takes it, and then our bishop, which we've assigned the vital task of winning the rook, gets distracted defending. Instead we simply drop the knight back to e7. The point isn't to activate it; we're after far greener pastures — the rook. White's best is the knight to c3, cutting his losses to just the knight.
White does find the knight to c3, and we take it, capturing on c3 — good defence, but we're winning the rook.
White saves the rook to b1. Now — White's king is very weak: the move g4 has opened a direct avenue toward it.

We exploit that avenue with d4 — a move doing several jobs at once: it shelters our bishop on c3, advances our passed pawn, and prepares the queen to c6, setting up a discovered check. It also opens the path for our e7-knight to reroute via d5 and even into e3 when we're ready.

Here's a system where White plays the knight to b3 — with your new understanding, what's the point of spending two moves on that? To discourage c5. In that game Black plays the knight to h6 as early as move six, unafraid of White taking on h6, because it opens the g-file: Black castles long and uses that file, and removing Black's dark-squared bishop actually makes it HARDER for White to stop c5. The same ideas recur across most Caro lines — that's what makes it so rewarding: learn the ideas once and they transfer.

node.idea: f3 — the Fantasy Variation. Instead of the usual moves, we bolster e4 with the f-pawn and dare Black to try to punish the loosened kingside.
Black develops with a knight to d7 — and I'll be honest, I've never seen it here. It isn't a top move; I'd call it an inaccuracy: passive, and it does nothing to contest the center.

So we close it down with e5. I want to give you a broad tour of a closed-center position — a lot of players feel lost when the center locks, as if they're just shuffling pieces. In truth these are some of the richest games in chess, because they force play on the flanks, where the most beautiful and tactical ideas live. Our next job is to reinforce both links of the d4-e5 chain, because Black will attack it with pawns.
c5 hits the base of our chain — a classic French break. Black can also come from the other side with f6, which is exactly why I like f4.
c3, a no-brainer, propping up d4. We absolutely don't want the chain to dissolve this early with no pieces out — that chain is the only thing standing between us and disaster.

The knight belongs on f3; a knight to e2 would be awkward and would bury the light-squared bishop. Black's queen to c7 is a bit pointless — it doesn't even threaten a capture on d4, since we recapture and the c1 bishop is guarded by our own queen. So we keep developing, and the move order is flexible.

I'll bring the bishop to d3 first, since we're lagging in development and haven't moved a minor piece — and it also keeps the knight-to-e2 option alive, which is far more palatable once the bishop is already out.
Black plays e6, and we keep everything as flexible as possible — with the opponent playing so unambitiously, we can leave many developing paths open.
Now f4 — the maximally ambitious, textbook move, grabbing space and taking the fight to the opponent.
Black plays g6. The c1 bishop starts complaining that it's staring at its own pawn, but it has fine squares on e3 or d2 — not every piece has to climb Everest at once.
On e3 the bishop actually does a great job further supporting the chain, which we want rock-solid. But first, the knight to f3 — let's get the pieces we know how to place out.

Black's knight goes to e7, heading for f5 to press d4 in true French fashion. Don't be tempted by g4 to stop it — that's far too cavalier with so little developed. After g4, h5 is a classic response: we can't answer h3, Black captures on g4, and the h1 rook hangs, so g4 hands Black a huge f5 outpost instead of denying one.

So the bishop to e3 — and the subtlety is that when the knight lands on f5, our bishop slides back to f2. Castle first and that retreat to e3 is no longer available; the small developmental detail decides how smoothly the game runs.
The knight comes to f5, and the bishop drops to f2, first overprotecting the d4 pawn and, much later, eyeing a route into Black's position.
A bishop maneuver to h4 and f6 is a common infiltration, especially against a fianchetto with a bishop fianchettoed to g7.
We castle and keep developing. The h5 push is typical for this structure.

h5 does prevent g4, but it creates major dark-square weaknesses — notice the outpost on g5. That doesn't mean we leap there now; a knight to g5 lets Black trade and fill the holes. Later, though, g5 becomes a transit square, and a plan of trading on f5 and swinging the bishop to h4 hands our queen a swarm of juicy kingside outposts. With the center closed we have time — the position simply doesn't change fast.

A knight to a3 is a dead-end after a6, so instead the b1 knight goes to d2 — toward the center, going nowhere in particular yet, a Frankfurt-airport move you never regret. Remember, closed positions offer two broad plans: arrange your pieces to blast the center open, or maneuver on a flank.

Black plays a queen to b6. Here's our plan: rip the whole thing open and bank on our more active pieces handling the chaos better. Not a capture on c5 — that just hands Black space and the e3 square. Instead c4, building a pawn box that guarantees the center will open, perhaps after first eliminating Black's only active piece with a capture on f5.

c4 it is — and we can delay the capture on f5, playing it a little later. And we're not afraid of losing b2: when you've castled on the opposite wing a single b-pawn almost never matters, and here our queenside stays intact — Black can't unravel it the way a b2-then-c3 collapse would.

The queen grabs b2, but it creates no threats and doesn't stop our central agenda. Trying to trap it with a queen to a4 and a rook to b1 fails to a strong resource, and we lack the queenside firepower anyway — so we keep our focus in the center and press to open it.

We start with a move we know is good — capturing on d5. If Black doesn't recapture, the pawn marches to d6 and it's horrific for him, so he'll take back, and then a capture on f5 to wreck his structure is the idea.
Black recaptures on d5, and we should be tempted to grab the knight on f5 — giving up our light-square control hurts, but it's a price well worth paying.
So we capture on f5, taking the knight, while we still can, trading our good bishop to shatter Black's kingside pawns.
Black recaptures with the g-pawn, and now we complete the opening of the center.

We finish it with a capture on c5 — the center is now fully open, so we shift from luxurious positional play to hunting tactics. Black still hasn't developed his queenside, and we've invested a pawn, so we must hit the gas.
Black recaptures on c5. Only a couple of moves stand between him and consolidating that extra pawn, so we accelerate — and a bishop to d4 catches my eye, x-raying the rook.

The bishop to d4 hits the queen, centralizes beautifully, and prepares an e6 discovery against the rook — good as a plan and good as a plain developing move. It also shoos away that b2 queen, which was cramping our coordination.
Black shuffles the queen to a3, but our reply to almost anything here is e6 — and our opponent is defending this fantastically, making us work.
e6 is nearly automatic: without it, Black plants a knight into e6 and keeps the center closed.
Black plays a rook to g8 — and that, I think, is the decisive mistake.
Because now, without a second thought, we capture on f7, dragging the king out into the open.

The king is forced to f7 — f6 was the only survival try. Now the firepower tells: a knight to e5 with check, and lines flow, though a queen grab on h5 with check isn't yet mate because the king slips to d8.
A knight to e5 with check. Black could try the king to g6, using the king itself as a defender, but there's no reason to overcomplicate — the knight to e5 is clean.

The king walks out to e6. This looks like hara-kiri for Black. One pitfall for us is a rook to e1 — there's a knight jump to e4 in reply, and if the king ever steps to d6 a knight to c4 forks king and queen. No need for any of that: the simplest move is to capture the h-pawn, not for the pawn but to route the queen toward f7.

The queen takes h5, Black defends with a rook to f8, and the queen checks from h6 — the whole point being to prevent a bishop to f6. Compare your checks: two similar-looking checks rarely do the same job.
The rook is driven to f6, and remember — even mid-attack you're allowed to win material. Players fixate on delivering mate; here the rook sits under the bishop's x-ray.
A queen to g7 — using the weakness of Black's king to go after his pieces, because a king so exposed forces the defenders onto vulnerable squares.
Black finds the only move, a queen to b4, holding things together; a queen check on g8 and the king to d6 leaves us with a beautiful win to find.

A knight to f3 is what I like — it gives away nothing, prepares a knight to g5, and safely defends the bishop. A resilient defender makes you work, but at most levels the position collapses in a couple of moves.
Crucially, we've sacrificed nothing — it's plus eleven. If Black plays a knight to e4 to take the sting out of a knight to g5, the top computer move is a wonderfully quiet one.
Just a rook to c1 — bringing a piece into the attack and cutting the king off from its escape. These quiet inclusions are the moves people won't make when attacking, yet they decide the game.
Against a bishop to d7 we simply play a rook to c7.
The rook to c7 — its added presence overwhelms Black's defense.
Black tries a rook to d8, and the engine's move is striking.
A knight to f7.
After the rook takes it, a queen to e5 is checkmate — a pretty little concept, everything protected, completely one-sided.

As an Accelerated Dragon player we stay consistent and fianchetto with g6 anyway — the bishop belongs on the long diagonal whether or not White ever takes on c6.

We take with the d-pawn, not the b-pawn. Recapturing toward the center looks natural, but taking with the d-pawn opens the d-file for our rooks and frees the light-squared bishop — activity over a tidy pawn mass.
Now the pawn to e5 clamps the center and grabs kingside space, freezing White's structure before he can expand.
The knight belongs on e7 for two reasons: it keeps the e5-pawn from hanging, and it leaves the a-pawn free so we can strike with a5 later. It blocks the bishop only for a moment.
White plays c3, but he isn't actually threatening d4 yet — a bit of simple counting shows the center holds, and even if he pushed d4 it would only open our long-diagonal bishop.

The pawn on d3 is weak, and that's our target. There are two ways to pressure a fixed weakness: the brute-force pawn lever with c4 or the bishop swinging to a6, and doubling rooks on the d-file. We aim to do both.
The bishop reaches a6, bearing down the diagonal at the weak pawn — the first half of the plan.
f6 here is fine, despite the old rule against it — White simply has no pieces to exploit the weakened square, so it's a safe, temporary loosening.
The queen to d7 links up with a rook to d8 — piling every piece we can onto the d3 weakness. Win that pawn and his position caves.
We kick the knight off its active post with b5.
The knight slinks back to a3, buried and passive; it did block our light-squared bishop, but a knight on the rim is a fair trade for that.
Now b4 is finally right. A move earlier it would have run into a nasty queen check on b3; with that resource gone we push it.
White reroutes to c2, which removes the b3-check idea for good — so b4 is safe and pairs perfectly with a rook to d8.

With the push to d4 the whole battle now revolves around that pawn.
We double on the d-file, rook to d7, stacking the pressure exactly where White is weakest.
The pawn to c4 walls the knight in — his knight on a3 is now buried alive with no way out, effectively leaving us a piece up in the fight for the d-file.
We answer his regrouping in kind, rerouting our own knight to d6 — a superb square eyeing c4 and e4 and reinforcing the pressure.
a6 cements the bishop on a light square defended by a pawn, so it can never be harassed off the diagonal.
The knight steps to f7, unmasking the rook so it bears straight down the file.
When White releases the tension we recapture with the f-pawn, not the knight — taking with the knight would have surrendered the d4-square, and control of d4 is the whole point of the position.
The rook drops onto d3 — a dream outpost deep in White's camp, jamming his pieces and paralyzing the position.

So the knight goes back to f6 — a retreat in name only, redeploying toward an outpost on d5 or the strong g4-square, and keeping pieces on makes it harder for White to breathe. White jumps the knight to c4, where it feels a touch loose — the queen to c7 or d5 comes to mind.
We play the queen to c7, keeping the tension. This is a universal, very safe construction — the c6-pawn guards against knight jumps to b5 and d5, and the queen sits comfortably.

White plays a rook to d1. We don't take the bishop — our central knight is a monster, defended by the pawn and blanketing the position. The theme is keeping the tension, not trading unless forced, and it's time to start the kingside plan of e5, f5, and e4. The pawn to h5 threatening the bishop to g4 is met simply by h3, so it's not worth the weakening.
So the pawn to e5 — kicking the d4-knight, with f5 and then e4 or f4 to ram our pawns down the board. Notice how vulnerable White's queen is compared to ours.

White retreats the knight to b3, and we push the pawn to f5. White's pieces are like unanchored bowling pins — we just keep rolling them back with our pawns, while our own pieces are well anchored, either far away or protected by a pawn.

node.idea: The queen's knight to c3 is a rare guest here. The rule of thumb against it: play the same line you'd choose in the open Sicilian, because White can still slide the king's knight out and push the d-pawn to transpose straight back into one. A Najdorf player answers with d6, a Taimanov or Kan player with e6 — pick the matching setup or you risk getting move-ordered into a line you don't actually play. For an Accelerated Dragon there's an underrated try that dodges a mountain of theory.

The immediate g6 flies under the radar. It sidesteps all the Nc6, Bb5 Rossolimo-style theory you'd otherwise have to know, and it's perfectly sound — a bishop sortie to b5 makes no sense against this move order.

White transposes into the Grand Prix Attack. It shares the DNA of the Closed Sicilian, but where the Closed version fianchettoes and plays positionally, the Grand Prix goes for the throat — the light-squared bishop swings to c4, often after a check on b5, to lean on the f7-square. It's a genuinely scary weapon against a less experienced Sicilian player.
We complete the fianchetto, exactly the setup we'd want whether we'd started with the knight or with g6.
Against the knight coming to f3 we assemble the structure regarded as Black's best answer to the Grand Prix — and it doubles as a recipe against the Closed Sicilian too.
First things first, develop. The queen's knight to c6 is the most flexible start — it commits to no pawn move yet and simply waits to see where White's pieces go.

Now the bishop on b5 tells us more about White's plan. The key is what to avoid: don't reach for e6. After e6, White snaps the knight and rams the pawn to e5, leaving Black riddled with dark-square holes on d6, f6 and c5 — a miserable version to defend.

Instead the immediate knight to d4 flies under the radar. It's the same motif you meet in the Trompowsky: a bishop parked on b5 is simply loose, vulnerable to a knight leaping into d4. We ask the bishop a question right away.

White castles and turns the tables — daring us to take the bishop. We're delighted to. That light-squared bishop, once it lands on c4 bearing down on f7, is the Grand Prix's main attacker, the bishop from hell in these positions. Off it comes.
So we capture, eliminating the bishop before it can do any damage.

White recaptures and we hit our second decision. The instinct against a knight on b5 is to shove it back with a6 — but resist. The knight isn't threatening c7 or d7; it's just sitting there, undefended and harmless. Save a6 for a rainy day, because playing it now only invites the knight back to c3 where it clamps the d5-square. Leave it be and finish our development.

If we develop the king's knight to f6 immediately, White gets to push e5 and jam a pawn into our position. So we prep with d6 first — the classic Sicilian move, staking out the central squares and taking e5 off the table.

Qe1 is the flexible maneuver — it commits to nothing but eyes the Qh4 swing, exactly as in the Grand Prix Attack.

Ne4 is my favorite kind of move — aggressive and prophylactic at once: it heads for f6 while quietly stopping Nb4. Those double-duty moves are the most annoying to face.
c3 kicks the knight and covers d4 — but a move that allows a discovery needs concrete checking, so make sure you've counted every knight jump before you play it.

g4 chases the knight and grabs space. Nobody should worry about pushing pawns in front of the king here — Black is far too passive to ever exploit it.
h3 supports the advance, and note Black is weak on c5 too — the position is essentially zugzwang-bound; White is winning on strategy alone.
The knockout is all about order: g5 first would hand Black a stronghold on f5, so start with Nf6-check. If Black takes twice, g5 wins the knight; otherwise Qh4 or f5 crashes through.
Black has to give up the piece — a full extra minor and every dark square, decisive.
Qf2 sets up Bc5 and coordinates the rooks — patient improvement while up material.

f4 — so this is an attempt at a Stonewall, which has been around a while; White wants to play e3 and c3. There are a couple of things we can do against it: one is d5, controlling the e4-square,

but I don't like playing d5 against the Stonewall. Even if you're not a King's-Indian player, I like the King's-Indian setup against it — you don't have to be a King's-Indian player; White should really meet it with c5, then c-takes and d-takes, to be able to play the King's Indian. So
let's make the standard King's-Indian moves — the bishop to g7.
and castle — the order doesn't matter; we'll play d6, though castling first was a little more flexible.

The bishop to d3. The funny thing is I'm going to allow White to play e4 next, which would be a Pirc up a tempo — I kind of play the Pirc anyway, so I don't mind, and someone who plays d4 and f4 won't be familiar with the Pirc's ideas for White.
So we castle — I'm not afraid of e4.

What's the benefit of the pawn on d6 rather than d5? What idea does d6 prepare? You could play c5, but that's not my favourite — c5 can just be met with c3, much like the London. What we need to prepare is e5 — not immediately, we can't yet — we prepare it with the knight to c6. The point is that when we play e5 we
cause a much bigger explosion in the centre, because we attack both pawns and threaten a fork — so e5 does a lot more than c5 here. Let's get our knight out.

And now we're ready to play e5. You might look at this and say White has three attackers and only two defenders — but if you calculate further, to win the pawn White has to totally ruin his structure,
and we'll win the e5-pawn back very easily. I can show this in more detail after the game, but we can safely play e5 without worrying about losing a pawn.

The rook to e8 is a pretty inoffensive move we can always throw in, reinforcing the threat of e4, and maybe we play e-takes-d later and open the e-file. Actually, first we should develop our bishop — I know some of you think of the bishop to g4, but then h3 chases it away; the alternate way is b6 and the bishop to b7, fianchettoing the other bishop and aiming at the e4-square. This is a pawn sacrifice — let's see if our opponent figures out how to win it. The knight to g5 is an intimidating-looking move, but is it scary? I don't see what it threatens, so we continue developing; probably the bishop to c4, but then we simply defend the pawn with the rook to e7. The knight to d5 would give up f7 potentially, so be careful — always consider what you're opening and closing when you move a knight. g4 is a mistake. Should we take the knight? Yes — we take on g5, because that exposes an attack on the other knight: after the knight takes and the queen takes g5, White has to recapture our knight with his knight, which takes the pressure off the f-pawn; and one step further, the knight takes e4 is a very natural, strong King's-Indian continuation. Am I afraid of the knight taking f7? I calculated it — if he plays it, f5 chases the knight away, and then e4, or the capture on d4 pushing his pieces back. Now, our opponent is contemplating the knight takes f7 — an intermezzo that attacks the queen, and White has two attackers on our knight over on e4, so wherever our queen goes, even to h4, it appears White can capture the knight with the bishop. But I calculated — wait, maybe I miscalculated; we might have to go into an endgame I don't want. He out-calculated me. I was intending the queen to h4, and what I missed is the smothered-mate idea: after the bishop takes c4, the queen to b3 sets up an unstoppable discovered check against the king and a potential smothered mate. So the knight takes e4 was simply a mistake — I underestimated the knight to f7. So after the capture, since the bishop takes e4 is a big mistake because of the queen to b3, is there an alternative? We have to take the bishop with the queen, offering a queen trade; then he takes on e5, basically everything trades, and it's essentially a dead draw — but we'll try to win that endgame. We panic and bite the bullet, because otherwise the bishop takes c4 and he finds the queen to b3 and we're busted. Now I have to prove my mettle by winning an endgame nearly devoid of chances. The queen to f2, leaving our battery intact — I think this just loses. We can play e-takes-d4, but then there might be the knight to h6 with check, a nasty idea that forces a trade; then we pin the knight. We're not threatening the rook takes f7 — some of you might think we are, but then the queen takes f7 with check — what we're threatening is the bishop from b7 to d5, picking off the knight, which I don't think can be defended. I'm disappointed in my play — maybe fianchettoing the bishop was fundamentally too slow. People in the seventeen-, eighteen-hundred range make this kind of mistake often; there's a psychology name for it, like walking to the wrong floor of a building out of habit. Something even better than the bishop to d5: because after the bishop to d5, the rook to e1 gives us something to deal with — we want to attack the knight without allowing the rook to e1, so the queen to d5. That violates my rule of accomplishing tasks with the lowest-value piece, but it's an exception, because the queen is vulnerable to begin with — so we do two things at once, making the queen safer and attacking and winning the knight. This is a lesson in flexibility: players think they must keep attacking no matter what and rule out all queen trades, and they ignore what's actually going on — that I now have this battery and there's no longer any attack; that inflexibility makes you lose objectivity. Let's snag the queen and convert with discipline. What we shouldn't do is the bishop takes e5 — I don't like giving away the dark-squared bishop, because those with a keen tactical eye see that the bishop to h6 could become a problem, with White creating mate threats on f8. So two options: the rook to f8, trading one pair of rooks; and c5, undermining the knight, which is defended by the pawn — the undermining concept is so important. And after the rook to f1, ask how the position has changed and don't lose sight of the whole board: the a2-pawn is now hanging, so after the trade you can safely take on a2 and start grabbing everything on the queenside. The knight to f3 — he brought the knight back himself, a good move. We have a fancy move available, but there are so many good moves I struggle to verbalise — g5 and then g4. The move I'd play in a classical game is c5. You might say the point was to undermine the knight, which we've done — but I want to get rid of the d-pawn so our queen gets more real estate in the centre: d-takes-c5, the queen takes e5, pinning the rook and threatening to double-capture on f3 because of the pin. That d4-pawn holds us back, so get rid of it and open files — the more files open, the easier it is to convert the extra queen. Our dark-squared bishop isn't good and won't be even after the trade, since there'll be a c3-pawn staring at it, but at least it controls the d4-square. I have a great high-level example of an international master who did exactly this against me — instructive on how chess psychology can be used against people, even to defend bad positions. The rook to e1 — time to grab; pinned. I briefly checked the rook to e8 with check, making sure there's nothing after the king to f7 — anytime you abandon the back rank, always check fast. The rook to f1 — b4 is a threat, so we kind of have to take; there's a fancy move, but let's keep it simple and take. After the rook takes f2, I really like the bishop from g7 to e5 idea. The bishop takes h2 — how did I see it? A lot of people passively notice the pin and think, can I attack the rook with the bishop to d4? No, there's a pawn on c3 — and they file it away. I don't stop there: the pin means the king is defending the rook, so it's overloaded, and going after the h2-pawn could be an overloading tactic. The queen takes f2 is also a fork, but just winning the rook is already enough — the point is that high-level players don't just see the tactical phenomenon, they understand how it can be used as a component in a combination. b4 — I saw this; we need to move the queen and defend the bishop, so the queen to e5 or d6; I like the queen to d6, because if the bishop to h6 happens, we can move our bishop back and sacrifice on f8 and keep the bishop; we can also give the queen to g3 with check and win the bishop. Actually the queen to h3 — this is just a fork.

This gives our knight a potential outpost on d4 — but a hole existing doesn't mean occupy it at once. We start with the knight to c6, not to play the knight to d4 next: it's too early, with nothing else developed.
The knight to f3 would just knock a d4-knight off. It's the long-term weakness that costs White later. We also get a massive diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.
We play g6 — though in a classical game I'd prefer e6 or the knight to f6, since g6 allows White to transition to main lines.

Let's go e6, basically playing a Queen's Gambit structure, except with the bishop outside the pawn chain. The problem with my loss of a tempo is that it gave him a chance to develop, with the queen coming to b3. Now this b7-pawn is hanging. The move you often want to avoid is b6 — it creates a lot of weaknesses on that side, look at the c6-square and the light squares b6 weakens, and White has the very nasty knight to e5; if that knight reaches e5 we come under real pressure. So logically, since b6 and g5 are a problem, I'll make a move that may look like a blunder: just take the knight on f3. The queen takes b7 is often possible in such positions, but here it's not as good as it looks — after the queen grabs b7, the knight to d7 is the usual move, but we can actually snatch the pawn on g2 with that same bishop, which is why he didn't go for it. Now, we want to have some fun — we don't want to play like a coward. I'm proposing that we sacrifice. What am I noticing? White's king won't be safe on the kingside, and it's very far from castling queenside; and here's the funny thing — if White takes on b7, that does our bidding for us, because if White then castles queenside, the open b-file gives us very nice play. So we pretend there's no threat and develop as normal. In such positions we rarely put the knight on c6, because we want the c5 pawn lever, so we develop the knight to d7 anyway — objectively probably unsound, but I've had a lot of success sacking b7 like this. What should we recapture with? Both pieces make sense: taking with the pawn preserves the structure; taking with the knight keeps the centre looser and more open, which I like — provocative chess, trying to get him to play e4 and weaken the centre. It's a Grünfeld-style approach where we don't occupy the centre with pawns, planning c5 at some point. Do we play g6? We might, but I don't think we need to — we can just get the bishop out to d6. Then e4, which I think is a mistake. Now the most energetic move — not the knight to f4, that blunders the knight — the knight to g4. We're not threatening to capture the bishop, but there's a hidden threat; we want to play as aggressively as possible, because White is extremely underdeveloped, and the way to exploit a development lead is to open the centre. We could play e5, but that gives the queen pressure on f7 — better to play c5. Then a3, and the knight drops back to c6, increasing the pressure on d4; the knight to d4 is coming and it's unstoppable, these knights are pouring out. e4 walked right into what we wanted, and c5 and a3 is also a mistake — this knight wants to be on c6, then on d4. d5 isn't dangerous; the knight to d4, and now the queen has to keep control of c2, so it goes back, and we grab the pawn, weakening his centre even further — this is close to losing for White. The queen to h4 is a move to keep in mind, but it does nothing yet. Taking on d5 makes sense — weaken his centre and open the e-file, and later we can put a rook to e8. If I were White I'd seriously consider not recapturing, but he recaptures. This is an instructive moment: people get tempted to do something immediate, but the best approach is to complete your development — nothing good happens when only one piece is developed; that knight is great, but without the other pieces and a safe king it's hard to do what we want. So the bishop to d6 — this requires patience — then castle, and only then start thinking about concrete actions. Do we defend that knight, or allow White to capture it on d4? The answer is no, we don't need to defend it — let him take it — because this bishop is the only thing standing in the way of us dominating the e-file; if White takes on d4 twice, we simply put a rook to e8, and this knight on d7 can jump to c5 and perhaps to b3 later. We're essentially replacing one advantage with another — transforming your advantage is one of the hardest things to master, because visually you look at the knight and want to preserve it. Now, which piece to activate? The bishop to e5 would block the e-file — no; the rook to c8 allows the knight to e4; so the knight to c5, threatening the knight to b3, and taking the sting out of a potential g4 — the knight is excellently placed on c5 even if we never reach b3. We certainly don't play the knight to b3 now, because that blunders checkmate in one; we don't have many ways to meet that mate threat, but f6 is perfectly acceptable — it blunts the queen and creates a stronghold on e5. The bishop to f8 was possible, but why overload the bishop? The queen to d1, and White's king is basically busted. When you're attacking, take free material that lies by the side of the road, so if the attack fizzles you still have something to fall back on — the bishop is coming back to e5, a great square, so we grab a pawn along the way first. White is defending well and making it hard, but now the material is equal and he has nothing to show for it, and our pieces are beautifully placed. The only piece we haven't activated is the queen — reverse-engineer where it belongs: the queen to b6 isn't as good because of b4; I want the queen on the kingside where everything is abandoned, so the queen to d7, heading for h3. We could also play f5, opening the path to h4 — equally good. King to f1. Before the queen goes to h3, I'll start with the bishop to f4 — you'll understand the idea soon — then the queen to h3, and if I've calculated correctly we're winning. I actually missed one detail and got a bit bamboozled; rather than take the bishop and try to mate, it's better just to restore the material balance and win positionally. Snag another pawn — now we're up a pawn, and Black is still winning pretty handily. One detail: if White ever captures on f6 with the queen, trying to use the pin, we have a trick — we can 'blunder' the f6-pawn and play the queen takes g2, taking the rook with check so the queen is no longer pinned. Then g4, an excellent move — we take it; the rook to c8 was actually bad, there was an insane idea White had there. Then the bishop to d6. We could take and take on e4, but then the queen to b3 wins our bishop — so instead we drop the bishop back to e6 and blockade with the rook to e8, trying to win the pawn; or the bishop to e7, getting it out of the danger zone. I like blockading the passed pawn so nothing can happen with promotion. Then the bishop to c4 — be careful: although it's not possible right now, a move like the queen to d3 would be dangerous, and the queen to a4 is the same concept, because if we move our bishop he pins our queen and wins. So we defend the bishop with the queen and sidestep the pin: the queen to d6 — better than the queen to e7, because now we have the idea of mating him on d1 if the queen ever loses control of that square. The king to f8 is interesting, but the king to h8 is much safer, and the queen to f7 here is a very common blunder that misses the mate. e5 seems to be panic — we take the pawn, up a ton, and it's winning. King to g1. Remember the queen to f7 is a real threat, so the queen has done its job on d6 — we keep the bishop protected and cover f7 with the queen to e7. Then a6, accomplishing our main plan, and White can resign, because the bishop is actually trapped: the bishop to a4, b5, and White loses not only the bishop but the pawn too. A good game, very well played by our opponent, who climbed back

Let's play positionally — e6, heading for the Nimzo.

One misconception: the Nimzo proper is only the knight to c3 met by the bishop to b4. Against anything else we shift to a Queen's-Indian or Bogo setup. White's e3 is passive but solid — it does box in his own bishop, and the ideal companion here is the Queen's-Indian plan with b6.

Why not check on b4 now? The bishop check is most effective specifically against the knight once it commits to c3; here White just interposes on d2 and we lose the structure-wrecking capture. So b6 instead — d5 transposing into a favourable Queen's Gambit Declined was also fine.
We fianchetto the bishop, and note the lovely control it gives us over the e4-square.

Now d5 to stake out the centre — a chance to explain the pawn as an extension of the bishop. It looks like d5 buries our own bishop, and it does restrict it for the moment. But the aim is control of central squares: if we later plant a piece on e4 and recapture with a pawn, the bishop ends up defending that pawn — and we can always take on c4 to reopen the diagonal. No rush; complete development first.
The bishop belongs on d6 — now both bishops are trained on White's king, so make a mental note to watch for tactics as the game opens.
We've got very nice central control. White's e4 break isn't a threat — we outnumber it three defenders to two attackers.
The queen's knight goes to d7, never c6 — c6 would block our own c-pawn and hem the bishop in further. And a6 is often useful to take the sting out of a knight jump to b5.

Here's the strategic engine of the position. Rather than the passive a6, we answer the knight-to-b5 threat with c5, turning up the temperature in the centre — and if the knight does jump to b5 we simply tuck the bishop back to b8, keeping it on its beautiful diagonal. Recapture with the pawn to preserve our central integrity, and now a d4 break can open that bishop with devastating effect — this is potential energy, the bishop coiled behind its own pawn. The calculation lesson runs through everything that follows: don't cash in too soon. Grabbing on f3 was more complicated than it looked, so keep every piece maximally active and hunt for a real knockout instead. There's a Greek-gift sacrifice in the air — the bishop crashing on h2, the knight to g4, and a queen infiltration exploiting an undefended f2 — and an all-hands-on-deck effort where even the sleepy knight must join. Control the e2-square so the king can never make its dash to safety, and the net closes with a rook to e2 and mate. The theme is converting potential energy into kinetic: often the simplest continuation is strongest because it keeps all your trumps.

Black — the whole point of the Colle is to preserve the light-squared bishop, not to trade it. We don't have to rush with the bishop taking d3; there's a nice positional move some of you might not see intuitively. Many of you are thinking of the bishop to g6, but there's another way to keep the tension and offer a change of pawn structure that I really like —
not g6 but e6. That's the move I enjoy here, and in the event of a trade we get this massive structure.

e-takes-f5, and now I can explain what to do in this structure. The queen to d3 is a good move, and we need to be careful tactically for one move: if we play g6, those with a sharp eye see the queen to b5 with check, hitting the king and the pawn — same after the knight to e4, there's the queen to b5 with check — so we play the queen to d7 to defend both at once. We need to stay careful for a couple of moves, because the knight is coming to e5. You could play the knight to c6, but if you remember, I don't like blocking the c-pawn in Queen's-Pawn openings, so I much prefer the bishop to d6; and if g5, we just take it and play g4 — not a good trade for White. He castles; we also castle; then we play the rook to e8, to prevent g5 and clamp down even further on the centre. This is the whole zen of our strategy: it's hard for White to free himself. Good players know how to handle these positions with White, but in the fourteen-, fifteen-hundred range people aren't very good at dealing with being cramped. The bishop to a3 is White's idea — one of the best against this setup. What do we do now? Several improving moves: the rook to e8, centralising the knight on e4, or c5 at some point — but I actually prefer to put the pawn on c6, because c5 defeats the purpose: opening the centre goes against what we're trying to do and gives the opponent breathing room. So I like either the rook to e8 or the knight to e4, but the most flexible is the rook to e8. g6 isn't bad, but it's not necessary — our queen defends the pawn just fine. Is the knight to e4 still good? Absolutely, because if he takes it, we recapture with a fork; then we play c6 to protect the d5-pawn. And where does the queenside knight go? The position is closed, so no rush — for instance after c6 we can go the knight to a6 and back to c7, a route you've seen before. So c6, reinforcing the d5-pawn. The other approach: the queen has done its job on d7 and now looks awkward there, so we move it aside and open the d7-square for the knight — more palatable to me than the knight to a6. Where to move the queen? The primary point is to free d7 for the knight, but if you're moving it anyway, accomplish something else too — White's king isn't the safest piece and White is very passive, so an attack could be a way to play. So I like the queen to e6 — the queen to e7 is also fine, but I like e6 because the queen can swing to h6, a queen lift; not saying we will, but we might. Which brings up an important point: playing positionally doesn't mean you can't attack — you can do both, and transition to a king attack at the right moment. c4 — I think that's what we do now; we've fully improved, so what are we waiting for? Time for the queen lift, the queen to h6. We're not worried about the trade opening the c-file, because we have all the c-file squares well protected — his queen can't infiltrate. This closes things down even further and unties our hands for kingside action, and winter is coming for his king. g5 might run into g3; he plays g3 anyway. When you're attacking like this, think in terms of drawbacks — the drawback of g3 is that it weakens h3. Can we exploit it? Yes: we can put the queen coming to h3, and then bring the knight to g4, creating a situation where White is totally helpless, with one flimsy knight over on f3 saving him from death; there are also ideas of sacrificing on g3, though it's not as appetising here. Multiple approaches — we could lift the rook to h6 — but the best is the knight to f6 and the knight to g4. Why the queen to h3 first, rather than the knight to f6 immediately? Because White can sometimes play h4 and keep our queen out of h3. So we continue with the knight to f6, we see it does nothing, and White's position totally collapses. We could play the knight to g4 anyway, giving up f5 — but the f5-pawn is totally unimportant here. These situations with the queen coming to h3 and the knight landing on g4 are important to understand tactically: our objective is to distract the knight from f3, and only a knight can do that — the knight to g5. Our opponent plays resiliently — the knight to g1 makes it harder — but it was already over. Be flexible: one objective is removing that knight from f3, but there's also a brute-force approach, crashing through by overloading the h2-pawn. There's an idea with the rook to e6, the knight sitting on g5: if the queen takes f5, the simplest win is the knight takes f3, the knight recaptures, and then, noticing the alignment of the queen and knight, the knight to f6 wins the knight and mates; and if he doesn't take on f5, we play the rook to h6 and the knight takes h2 — and there's one cool idea, the knight takes h2, the knight recaptures, and it's mate; I've seen cases where people drop the knight back to f3, and then there's a cool tactic with the queen to h1.

node.idea: The bishop to g5 — the Trompowsky, named after the Brazilian Octavio Trompowsky. There's a misconception that only the knight to e4 works here; actually Black has many ways to equalize.
e6 and even g6 are reasonable, d5 is underrated, even c5 is playable — but I've always played the principled knight to e4.

At a lower level, h4 — the Hodgson variation, a very double-edged move — causes consternation. Its idea is simple: it defends the bishop, and if Black takes on g5, White recaptures with the h-pawn, opening the h-file (Black has the h7 pawn, restricting the rook) and creating a deep-freeze — the g5 pawn making it very hard for Black to ever fix the h7 weakness, since after h6 White takes and damages Black's kingside. So taking the bishop isn't best.

Black has many options; I'll play it simply with d5 — occupy the centre and toss the ball back. h4's drawback, beyond not developing, is that it commits White to an uncertain king: kingside castling is unlikely with the damage, queenside is risky with the knight on e4, and staying central is dubious.

The knight to d2 — he knows his theory. I don't want to take on g5, which plays into White's hands; instead I'll simply drop the knight back to f6 or d6, a symmetrical Queen's-Gambit-Declined-type position.
The knight back to f6. Moving the same piece three times seems wrong, but the centre is closed, so the effect is diminished — and White spent tempi on the weakening h4.

e3. The point of the knight's to-and-fro: we induced h4, provoking a serious kingside weakness, and now develop conventionally. We've been move-ordered into a reverse Queen's Gambit Declined — where White plays c4, we play c5 from the black side, but after c5 we must watch d takes c5.
Since White is developed, after c5, d takes c5, e6, White solidifies with b4 — so we start with the solid e6 and follow with c5 to contest and pressure White's centre.

The knight to e2. Let's play c5 — we can also throw in h6 to force the bishop to commit, but no rush; this pin isn't dangerous, since an easy test is whether the pinned piece is protected by a pawn, and it is.
We play c5, and White takes, capturing on c5.
We recapture with the bishop, capturing on c5 — precisely why we started with e6.
White's knights on e2 and d2 are passive; a3 is a good move, preparing b4. Many would auto-play a5, but not every idea must be prevented — b4 isn't a threat, just an idea; what does b4 actually do?

b4 chases our bishop from c5 — but the bishop is happy to drop to e7, ending the pin. So we develop the knight to c6. And after b4, that pawn becomes a target: we chisel with a5 once White's pawn is on b4 — the base of the chain, or sometimes the tip.
The knight to f4 — a perfect chance for the move I mentioned earlier: the bishop on g5 is now fully deprived of squares.
So it's time for h6, forcing White to trade the bishop for the knight, capturing on f6, letting our queen come to the active f6.
We recapture with the queen, capturing on f6. White has traded the dark-squared bishop, the pride of the Trompowsky — a great position for us.

The queen on f6 attacks b2 and pressures f2 — Black's already better. The knight to h5. We can grab the pawn on b2: people fear the queen getting trapped, but calculate concretely — after the queen takes b2, the rook to b1, our queen defends g7, so we drop it to e5, not c3 where the rook to b3 chases it; the central queen looks vulnerable to f4, but f4 gives up e3 with check.

The queen takes, capturing on b2. After the rook to b1, the queen to e5 — and if White chases with the knight, it severs the connection to the h5-knight, letting us take on h5. So we can safely take b2. Even if e5 were unavailable, taking on a3 would be fine — a king move to f8 isn't the end of the world.
The bishop to e2. We have ways to deal with g7 — g6 is the forcing option, or we simply castle. The king is safest on f8, surrounded by pawn cover; d7 walks into the d-file x-ray.

Castling kills two birds — it develops and protects g7. If I were White I'd contemplate g4 for kingside counterplay, using the uncastled king: the trope where the uncastled side can benefit from the h1-rook if the h-file opens — see Vukovic's Art of Attack.

f3 looks like it violates principle, but it does two jobs: it denies the knight the g4 jump that would dislodge our e3-bishop, and it further braces the center.
Now the attacking scheme: the queen to d2, so we can bring the bishop to h6 and trade off Black's fianchetto bishop — the guardian of the dark squares around his king.

We capture on f7 — eliminating one of the pawns that form his kingside foundation, exactly what we want before an attack.

node.idea: We've been playing d4 religiously — d4, and a Queen's Gambit.
He declines with c6 — the Slav; I don't think we've faced it, or maybe once.
introduce you to it. We can reach it through c-takes-d5, or through the knight to c3 — that's the Boor variation. Take on d5.
c-takes-d5 — the pure way of reaching this position.
Now we play the knight to c3. Whether we can play this line hinges on Black playing the main move, the knight to f6; if he plays the knight to c6, we have a second, also very dangerous idea.

The knight to f6. This is the Exchange Slav — following main-line theory it results in a very colourless position, a lot of pre-arranged draws; after the knight to f3 and the knight to c6 you get a symmetrical position that draws about seventy-five percent of the time. But recently people have started playing the Exchange Slav for a win — this line has been around for decades, informally named after a master who championed it, and it's the move f3.

If you're seeing this for the first time, this move should feel crazy — it violates essentially all principles of development. But that's exactly why it contains so much venom: people don't realise how dangerous Black's position can get, and how fast. Black has several ways to equalise, but the vast majority of players below 2200, and even 2000s, get completely lost in the complications. The idea of f3 should be obvious — to occupy the centre with e4 — but that's only the tip of the iceberg. Most people here play the knight to c6, which isn't necessarily bad, but really lets us carry out the main idea. It's not played at the highest level, because strong players know how to neutralise f3 — I'll show that after the game — and the critical move is not the bishop to f5. I'm not a specialist in the Boor, so our opponent might make a move I don't know.
The knight to c6 — so we ignore it and

continue with our plan, e4. Here you start to understand the main idea. It may seem d-takes-e4 wins a pawn — d-takes-e4, f-takes-e4, Black has two attackers on d4 and White only one defender, so the queen takes d4 wins a central pawn and offers a queen trade. But the point is that after d-takes-e4, you play d5 — an intermezzo a lot of players miss — leading to a very

dangerous position for Black: we play d5, force the knight off c6, and only then recapture on e4, getting a major pawn mass. But all of that is moot, because Black has played e5 — I don't know this move, which probably means it's not correct, but we'll think on our feet. Logically, White's choices are limited to really one move; it doesn't make much sense to
take on d5 — if we play e-takes-d5, at the very least Black takes the pawn on d4, establishing a knight in the centre. So the only reasonable move is d-takes-e5.

The knight takes e5 — a critical moment. A couple of candidate moves jump out. The most obvious is e-takes-d5, winning a pawn — but the drawback is that our development isn't great, the main flaw of the Boor. After e-takes-d5 I'm worried about the bishop to c5, developing to a really nice square, preventing us from castling. So set e-takes-d5 aside. Noticing this knight configuration should lead to a typical, universal idea: play f4 to chase one knight away, then e5 to drive the wedge and chase the other, creating a central pawn chain — that looks a lot more appealing than taking on d5. So I think f4 is correct. Why not develop the bishop while doing the same? Because

the bishop to f4 — if the knight drops back to g6, the bishop on f4 will be hanging; doing it with the pawn is generally safer. Let's go f4 — I'm confident it's best, which probably means it's wrong, but at least it makes logical sense. The bishop to g4 isn't dangerous, that's just one-move-itis.

The bishop to g4 simply creates a one-move threat against the queen, which we parry a million ways — the queen to b3 or the queen to a4 with check. Now, the fact that he's played the knight to c6 increases the appeal of taking on d5, because now it comes with tempo. After e-takes-d5, probably the knight to b4; but there's another interesting option, and a way to trade queens by force — even after the trade, though, our king could be a sitting duck. node.idea: The knight to c3 is a springboard into many systems — you'll know it as the Grand Prix introduction, but it's also a sly move order, because next move the other knight can come out and transpose straight back into an Open Sicilian. So how you answer it depends entirely on which Sicilian you play.

The underrated reply is an early a6 — most reach for a knight or a central pawn, but a6 makes wonderful sense for a Najdorf player and is a fine way to meet the Closed Sicilian and the Grand Prix alike.
The whole point of a6 is a quick b5 — grabbing queenside space early and, just as importantly, handing the light-squared bishop a natural home on the long diagonal.

Now the classic Sicilian setup: the central pawns settle on d6 and e6, a Scheveningen-style shell that controls a cluster of key squares. It looks passive but it's the heart and soul of the opening — and the knight can come out to f6 without fear, since the central break just runs into a loose bishop.
d6 gives maximum flexibility and, crucially, opens a d7 square for the other knight — in these structures it belongs there rather than on c6, where it would clumsily block the fianchettoed bishop.

This is the moment for the queen to c7, and it's played for layered reasons: it connects the rooks, and paired with the knight on d7 it double-guards e5 — smothering the central break that would otherwise be so dangerous. It's simply a better home than the back rank.

You'll feel the kinship with a hedgehog or hippo here — the d6-and-e6 pawns give that flavour, though it's really its own animal. And a castling caution: going long is risky, since those queenside pawns are hooks the opponent can lever open; short is safer, though long is never off the table.

A deliberately provocative move — h5 to stop the kingside pawn expansion, keeping the king parked in the centre for now. It's risky, but the aim is to be as annoying as possible and see how the opponent reacts.

When the opponent props the centre with c3, the thing to notice is that it has quietly weakened d3. And here's the key insight — you don't only attack a weak pawn with pieces, you undermine it with your own pawns. That points toward a c-pawn thrust to c4.
But capture on c3 first — playing the thrust immediately would leave the advanced b-pawn hanging. A small preparatory recapture, and then the undermining pawn goes in with a clear conscience.

Now the pawn arrives and the centre creaks. See how the minor pieces suddenly make sense — the queen guards the pawn, the bishop and knight both rake e4, and where they were biting on granite before, d3 is now a glaring weakness. That's the danger of shrinking your own pawn chain: the fewer links, the easier it is to undermine.

Don't snatch the weak pawn on reflex — the move is a knight to c5, bringing a piece into the attack and piling on d3, now genuinely threatening the capture. If the pawn advances to dodge, the central capture on e4 forces matters.

And a permission worth hearing: you're allowed not to castle at all. When the centre is closed and both wings look dangerous, keeping the king in the middle can be the lesser evil — the only real cost is that the rooks stay disconnected, which is rarely mission-critical.

The centre bursts open, and now it's pure order of operations. Trade on g2 first — that eliminates the bishop headache, and if the opponent grabs the knight the rook is simply captured with an extra exchange in hand. Clear the simplest question before weighing the harder one.

Of the remaining captures, the pawn recapture keeps the centre intact and stays a pawn up, and the pawn mass shields the king while the opponent's own shelter is far more exposed with the g-file about to open.

Recapturing toward the centre with the pawn is counter-intuitive but correct — in the Sicilian, keeping pawns pristine is rarely the priority. Shifting a pawn onto the f-file actually improves the structure: more pawns mean a safer king, it pries open the g-file as a direct road to the enemy king, and the front doubled pawn becomes a free battering ram to push while the one behind guards home. And it sets up the e4 outpost, the crown of the whole plan.

The pawn to d5 does three jobs at once — it cements the monster knight, springs the queen to life, and adds a third attacker to the target. And once you're this far ahead, remember the value of simplification: trading eliminates calculation, and don't fret about conceding a passed rook-pawn — it's a marathon from promotion while the centre steamrolls. In the technical phase, a pawn can even be used to cut the enemy bishop off a key square near the queening line.

The knight to f6 — a poor man's Scandi; technically it's in the Portuguese Gambit family, but White isn't supposed to keep the extra pawn. Why not simply c4? Because Black responds with c6, and after we either transpose to the Panov Caro-Kann or take greedily with the d-pawn, Black gets massive central control, a stronghold on d4, and White has a terrible light-squared bishop biting on c4 — tremendous compensation for the pawn.

So the line my coach taught me years ago — easy to learn, cool, and demonstrating positional principles: a check on b5. It's weird that our first move is with a bishop, but it develops with tempo, and if Black plays c6 now, we play the d-pawn takes c6, and since we haven't pushed to c4, c6 makes no sense for him. Black covers the check with the knight to d7 or —

the bishop to d7, which most people play. Is that bishop well placed? Absolutely not — it deprives the b8-knight of a square, cuts the queen off from the centre, and stands in the middle of everything, so we should leave it there. That's the idea: provoking a move that ends up counterproductive. You might reason we should play the bishop back to c4 to defend the pawn, but the bishop to c4 allows the bishop to g4, hitting the queen — and f3 isn't a move you want in the opening, and we might not keep the extra pawn on d5.
So not the queen to e2 or a4, which give Black a way out by letting him trade off that awkward piece on d7 — we physically move the bishop to e2 to stop the bishop to g4.
The idea is to stop the bishop to g4, and the reason we move the bishop at all is so that after a move like a4, Black doesn't rid himself of that awkward piece by agreeing to the bishop trade —
and then taking on d5, say with the queen. The queen to e2 does prevent the immediate bishop takes b5, which would be a fork, but after the queen to e2 Black just plays the knight takes d5 —

So we prevent that and grab the centre at the same time. You'd be right that c4 is coming — it won't be taken away from us — to push the knight from d5, giving us nice development and better central control, a small but stable advantage. Start with a simple developing move, the knight to f3, then castle, and only then c4. Conversely, that gives Black the extra option of the bishop to d6, intending to meet c4 with the knight to f4.

But we'll find a way around it. c5 is a good move — Black contests the centre and forces our hand. I said castle next, but the opportune moment has come to play c4, meeting Black in the centre instead of giving free rein, knocking the knight out immediately; if we castle instead, Black takes on d4 and plays the knight to c6, and by the time we play c4 it might be less effective.

If the knight to b4, we just play a3, not dangerous — though in some Alekhine and Scandi lines, with the light-squared bishop on f5, the knight to b4 is unpleasant, threatening a fork. Black plays the knight to f6. We can play the knight to c3 or castle. d5 might look appealing to create a passer, but it's totally innocuous — Black can trade, and an isolated passer this early is a liability, blockaded by the dark-squared bishop on d6. So instead of rushing forward, keep the tension with the knight to c3, and if the pawns trade we recapture with the knight, not the queen, which walks right into the knight to c6.

The knight to c6. Now d5 makes perfect sense — a tempo move hitting the knight, and, most importantly, denying Black the time to play the bishop to d6. We can prevent the bishop to d6 with the bishop to f4, a move we want anyway, because the bishop to d6 is the only way to blockade the passer; after the bishop to f4, the bishop to e7, d6, the bishop is almost trapped, and the passer becomes a great asset. g4 blunders a pawn, since we have two attackers on d4, so Black panics and blunders. The bishop to b4 is good; I don't like d6 here, since it doesn't gain a tempo and runs into the queen to b6 forcing a queen trade that leaves the pawn unguarded with the knight to e4 — too concrete — so we just castle, not a3. Like the e4-b6 game, we don't chase the bishop; we take the sting out of the pin by castling, and we want Black to take on c3 himself, losing a tempo compared to a3, and a3 would also take the a3-square from our dark-squared bishop, which gets a nice post there after the b-pawn recaptures. Then we develop the dark-squared bishop to g5 — this pin is underrated and very dangerous with Black castled kingside, the queen pressuring the knight, and the knight to g4 a huge threat; the bishop to e7 to escape the pin fails to d5 and d6. h6 — we can trade with the bishop takes f6, but it's early to trade queens when up a pawn, unlike up a piece where a queen trade helps simplify, so we keep the tension with the bishop to h4; if g5, that's amazing to provoke, weakening the knight and the king. The bishop to b7 walks into our idea, and the passer ends up deciding the game. The tricky bishop to c6 sets up an x-ray against the queen and precludes the take on c7, so we answer with the rook to d1, which protects the queen and the pawn at once and ends it, renewing the threat and keeping the bishop trapped. The queen to c6 is the most-popular-wrong-answer — we've won a minor piece and will trade queens soon. There's an elegant combination to win a second piece: the bishop takes f6, since the queen can't recapture, forcing the g-pawn to recapture, which opens the g-file for the queen to g3 with check — but not immediately, since the king goes to h8, so first the rook to d1 x-raying the queen, and if the bishop moves, the queen to g3 wins the queen; order of operations matters, since the rook to d1 first then the bishop takes f6 lets the queen recapture. The knight to e4 is terrible, since Black takes it hitting our queen. The rook to c7 — heavy pieces are bad defenders, and the bishop on d7 is on life support, so the knight to b5 plays itself; if he takes, the queen to g3 with check wins the queen and the rook. Let's finish in style: the queen to g3 with check, a discovery against the queen, we take the queen, and then take the rook, which has lost its support.

node.idea: The opponent trolls with a quiet e3 and d3 — a Hippo-style setup where White fianchettoes both bishops and tucks the knights back toward e2 and d2. It's worth knowing a sustainable way to punish these off-beat systems, because a lot of players either get scared or start stumbling against them.
Since White is handing us the centre, we grab it — the principled e5.
And we grab more with d5, taking a big share of the middle.

The preferred setup refrains from the knight to c6. Instead c6 builds a solid pawn chain, and the queen's knight reroutes Ruy-Lopez style via d7 and f8 to g6. Against such unambitious play, we have all the time in the world to improve.
The bishop to d6 complements c6 beautifully — London-style. It defends the e5-pawn while the pawn defends d5, giving us a super-compact, well-placed centre.
Castle kingside — never queenside here, that's far too adventurous. And note White's h3 is already a slight weakness; if g3 follows, it only creates another target on that wing.

Temper your expectations against these setups. I've seen countless games where one side plays an offbeat system and the other charges straight for the throat and loses — White isn't doing anything to lose the game. Be patient, get every piece out, and accept that breaking such a setup down takes time; it can't be done in the opening.
A typical queenside idea is to advance the a-pawn to poke and prod — and if White answers b4, we chip in with c5. With a closed centre, don't rule out moving the same pawn twice; there's no hurry.

Leave the light-squared bishop at home for now — a bishop to f5 walks into a g4 or e3-e4 expansion, and a bishop to e6 invites a knight jump to g5. We want to keep that bishop, because a key middlegame plan is pressuring the h3-pawn. So develop the knight to d7 instead.
The rook to e8 overprotects the e5-pawn — a good move in its own right — while we continue rerouting the knight toward g6.

If White's queen slides to e2, it signals a flirtation with castling queenside — a near-suicidal plan into our setup. So we play a5, telling the opponent: don't you dare castle into this, because we'll be ready to make mincemeat of that king.

node.idea: Against the early f-pawn thrust, the antidote is the immediate central break to d5 — and that's exactly why this move order isn't recommended; a genuine Grand Prix player would develop the knight first.
Don't recapture with the queen — instead develop the knight to f6, aiming to win the pawn back on your own terms rather than being dictated to.

The opponent defends the extra pawn, but that's no cause for alarm — the point is that the d4 square is now badly weakened. So switch into gambit mode: play e6, force the trade, and emerge with enormous compensation for the pawn. It's a well-known line every Sicilian player should carry.

The compensation, in one breath: huge central control anchored on d4, an enemy pawn stuck out like a sore thumb, a wretched bishop hemmed in behind its own pawns biting on granite, and an opponent's king with no safe haven, since the advanced pawn leaves castling short far from a cure. Spending a tempo on a rook-pawn move here is playing with fire when nothing is developed.
So develop with tempo — the bishop to d6, coming out with a hit on the weak pawn. Every developing move should also pose a threat when the opponent is this far behind.
The opponent ignores the threat, so simply grab the free pawn — it also unmasks a diagonal that can spell real trouble for the enemy king. Winning a pawn and opening a line in one is worth it.

Castle long for the adventurous game — the rook lands on the file already x-raying the queen and threatening a capture on c4, and above all it reinforces control of the key d4 square. Hold that square and everything is comfortable; now it's time to move in for the kill.

Don't rush the central knight jump — the move to reach for is the knight to g4, generating threats at the king with a capture on h2 looming and the knight eyeing an infiltration square. The storm clouds gather fast.

Here's the mating mechanism — the queen would mate on h2 but for the knight guarding it, and it can't leap over its own bishop. So distract the knight by planting a piece on d4 purely for tactics, not as an outpost; once it's captured, a bishop check on e3 forces the issue and the queen crashes into h2 for mate in two.
